tasks.title: Fix web UI initialization failures: health check URL, SPA routes, and query gates
tasks.closed_reason: Merged to dev after review approval. Verified health check now targets /api/health, /automation is included in SPA fallback routes, kspec validate had warnings only, and npm test passed (6690 passed, 3 skipped).

notes.author: @claude
notes.content:
## What

Three related issues in the web UI initialization and routing:

### 1. Health check URL mismatch (root cause)
`packages/web-ui/src/lib/stores/mode.svelte.ts:50` fetches `${DAEMON_API_BASE}/health` which resolves to `http://localhost:3456/health`. The actual endpoint is registered at `/api/health` (`packages/daemon/src/server.ts:276`). This always 404s.

The fallback chain then tries `/kspec-snapshot.json` (also 404s), and finally defaults to `mode = 'daemon'` with `initError` set. The app works but takes the slow path through two failed fetches, and the mode $state transitions through 'loading' → 'daemon' via the error fallback instead of the success path.

### 2. `/automation` missing from SPA fallback routes
`packages/daemon/src/server.ts:424-439` has a hardcoded `spaRoutes` array. `/automation` and `/automation/*` are missing. Hard refresh on `/automation` returns 404 because the static plugin can't find `automation/index.html` and there's no SPA fallback to serve `index.html`.

### 3. Redundant `!isStaticMode()` in query enabled gates
Several pages gate their TanStack Query `enabled` with `isProjectInitialized() && !isStaticMode()`. Pages using this pattern (agents, automation, dashboard, settings, session detail, board) don't load data on first client-side navigation. Pages using just `isProjectInitialized()` (tasks, reviews, specs, inbox, etc.) work fine.

The `!isStaticMode()` check reads the `mode` $state variable. Combined with the failed health check causing mode to take the slow fallback path, TanStack Query's Svelte 5 reactive evaluation of the `enabled` callback doesn't properly fire queries on initial mount. Navigating away and back re-mounts the component and queries work on the second try.

## Why

Issue 1 is a URL typo — the health endpoint was moved under `/api/` prefix but the client-side check wasn't updated.

Issue 2 is an omission — `/automation` route was added to SvelteKit but not to the daemon's SPA fallback list.

Issue 3 is redundant defensive code. `isProjectInitialized()` alone is sufficient: if `loadProjects()` succeeded (which it must have for `initialized` to be `true`), the daemon is up and we're in daemon mode. The `!isStaticMode()` guard protects against an impossible state (project initialized but in static mode) and its reactive dependency on `mode` causes the loading failure.

## How

### Fix 1: Health check URL
**File:** `packages/web-ui/src/lib/stores/mode.svelte.ts` line 50
- Change: `${DAEMON_API_BASE}/health` → `${DAEMON_API_BASE}/api/health`

### Fix 2: Add /automation to SPA routes
**File:** `packages/daemon/src/server.ts` lines 424-439
- Add `/automation` and `/automation/*` to the `spaRoutes` array

### Fix 3: Remove redundant !isStaticMode() from query gates
**Files affected (grep for `isProjectInitialized() && !isStaticMode()`):**
- `packages/web-ui/src/routes/automation/+page.svelte` — lines 45, 59, 66, 73
- `packages/web-ui/src/routes/agents/+page.svelte` — line 41
- `packages/web-ui/src/routes/+page.svelte` — line 94
- `packages/web-ui/src/routes/settings/+page.svelte` — lines 62, 68
- `packages/web-ui/src/routes/sessions/[id]/+page.svelte` — line 50
- `packages/web-ui/src/routes/tasks/board/+page.svelte` — line 57

Change all from `enabled: isProjectInitialized() && !isStaticMode()` to `enabled: isProjectInitialized()`. This matches the pattern used by all working pages (tasks, reviews, specs, inbox, triage, validate, workflows, observations).

Also remove unused `isStaticMode` imports from files where it was only used in the enabled gate.

### Verification
- Hard refresh on `/automation` → page loads (not 404)
- Navigate to `/agents` → data loads on first visit (no navigate-away-and-back needed)
- Navigate to `/automation` → data loads on first visit
- Dashboard, settings, session detail, board page all load on first visit
- Browser console: health check returns 200 (no more 404 on `/health`)
- Static mode build still works (isStaticMode() still used elsewhere for conditional rendering)

Updated the static analysis test in web-ui-tanstack-query.test.ts that expected !isStaticMode() in settings page. All 160 web-ui-tanstack-query tests pass. tasks.title: Clean up dangling references on item deletion
tasks.closed_reason: Merged dispatch/task/clean-up-dangling-references-on-item-deletion/01km6edz into dev at 17f4c13e291becc0d987480db43486e1c16bed8f after approved review 01KM6FB0WYQ18CBRP36A3ZG4JD. Verified kspec validate and npm test on the reviewed snapshot.

notes.author: @claude
notes.content:
## What

When an item is deleted via kspec item delete, other items that reference it via relationship fields (relates_to, depends_on, blocked_by, implements, tests, supersedes) are left with broken references. These are only caught later by kspec validate as errors. The deletion should clean up all dangling references as part of the same atomic operation.

Covers new ac-11 on @spec-item-delete-children.

## Why

Currently three broken relates_to references accumulated in meta.yaml from items that were deleted without cleanup. This is a recurring maintenance burden — every deletion risks leaving orphaned refs that pollute validation output. Task cancellation already does this for depends_on (src/cli/commands/task.ts:2282-2307), so there's proven precedent and an existing pattern to follow.

## How

### 1. Add a reference cleanup step to deleteSpecItem flow
**File:** src/cli/commands/item.ts (item delete handler, ~lines 1325-1496)

After the item(s) are identified for deletion but before the shadow commit:
- Load all spec items
- Scan every item's relationship fields for references matching any deleted ULID or slug
- Remove matching references from those fields
- Track cleanup count for reporting

The relationship fields to scan are the same ones that validateRefs() checks: relates_to, depends_on, blocked_by, implements, tests, supersedes.

### 2. Follow the task cancellation pattern
**Reference:** src/cli/commands/task.ts:2282-2307

The existing task cancel cleanup:
- Scans all tasks for depends_on refs to the cancelled task
- Removes them
- Adds a note explaining the removal
- Commits everything atomically

Apply the same approach: scan, remove, report count. Notes on affected items are optional but the count must be reported to the user (e.g., "Deleted @ref. Cleaned 3 references from 2 items.").

### 3. Handle cascade correctly
When --cascade deletes multiple items (A→B→C), collect ALL deleted ULIDs/slugs first, then do a single cleanup pass. Don't clean up references to B while B is also being deleted — that's wasted work.

### 4. Include in atomic commit
All reference removals must be part of the same shadow commit as the deletion itself (ac-6 already requires single commit for cascade). No intermediate state where refs are broken.

### Verification
- Delete an item that is referenced by other items' relates_to → refs cleaned, count reported
- Delete with --cascade where children are referenced → all refs cleaned in one pass
- kspec validate shows no errors after deletion
- JSON mode (--json) includes cleanup count in output
- Existing tests for ac-1 through ac-10 still pass

notes.author: @claude
notes.content:
Implemented ac-11: dangling reference cleanup on item deletion.

Added cleanupDanglingRefs() function in src/cli/commands/item.ts that runs after item deletion but before the shadow commit. It:
1. Collects all ULIDs and slugs of deleted items
2. Reloads remaining spec items and scans relationship fields (relates_to, depends_on, implements, tests, traits, supersedes)
3. Uses updateSpecItem() to remove matching references from spec items
4. Uses mutateTasksAtomically() to clean task references (depends_on, context, blocked_by, spec_ref)
5. Reports cleanup count in both human-readable and JSON output

Follows the existing task cancel cleanup pattern (src/cli/commands/task.ts:2282-2307). All reference removals are included in the same shadow commit as the deletion itself (satisfying ac-6).

Added 6 new tests covering: single ref cleanup, multi-item cleanup, cascade cleanup, JSON output, no-op case, and supersedes field cleanup. All 6696 tests pass.

tasks.title: Restore pre-block status on task unblock
tasks.closed_reason: Merged to dev at 0b83080a89d15bec8d00c46e33d52fc6c2597dd0. Restores prior task status on unblock, preserves original prior_status across repeated block calls, clears prior_status on reset/unblock, updates lifecycle help text, and adds regression coverage for in_progress/needs_work/pending_review/pending plus legacy fallback behavior.

notes.author: @claude
notes.content:
## What

kspec task unblock always sets status to pending regardless of what status the task had before being blocked. A task that was in_progress, needs_work, or pending_review before blocking should return to that status when unblocked.

Covers updated ACs:
- @state-blocked ac-1: task returns to the status it had before being blocked
- @task-unblock ac-1: task resumes from where it left off; if prior status is unknown, returns to pending

## Why

Dispatch workers that get blocked mid-work lose their in_progress state and fall back to pending on unblock. This means they get re-picked up as new work instead of continuing. Same issue for tasks in needs_work (fix cycle) or pending_review — unblocking drops important lifecycle context. We hit this with @01KM6BGY which was in needs_work but went to pending on unblock, requiring a manual patch to fix.

## How

### 1. Add a prior status field to the task schema
**File:** src/schema/task.ts

Add an optional field to store the status a task had before being blocked. This is only set when transitioning to blocked and cleared on unblock.

### 2. Record prior status in the block command
**File:** src/cli/commands/task.ts (block handler, ~line 2091-2153)

When transitioning to blocked, save the current status to the new field. The valid pre-block statuses are: pending, in_progress, needs_work, pending_review (completed and cancelled already reject blocking).

### 3. Restore prior status in the unblock command
**File:** src/cli/commands/task.ts (unblock handler, ~line 2155-2211)

On unblock, read the stored prior status and restore it instead of hardcoding pending. Clear the prior status field and blocked_by. Fall back to pending if the field is not set (backwards compat for tasks blocked before this change).

### 4. Update dispatch event payload
Both block and unblock already emit dispatch events with fromStatus/toStatus. The unblock event should now correctly report the restored status as toStatus instead of always reporting pending.

### Verification
- Block an in_progress task → unblock → status is in_progress
- Block a needs_work task → unblock → status is needs_work
- Block a pending_review task → unblock → status is pending_review
- Block a pending task → unblock → status is pending
- Unblock a task that was blocked before this change (no stored prior status) → status is pending
- kspec task get shows correct status after unblock
- Dispatch events report correct toStatus on unblock

Unblock handler restores prior_status (falls back to pending for backwards compat). Reset handler clears prior_status. Updated 2 existing tests and added 7 new tests covering all pre-block statuses (in_progress, needs_work, pending_review, pending), backwards compat, and JSON output. tasks.title: Implement task data manager module
tasks.description:
Create the task data manager as a single library module that will
become the exclusive interface for all task I/O operations.

Why: Task I/O is currently spread across loadAllTasks, saveTask,
mutateTaskAtomically, and mutateTasksAtomically in yaml.ts, with
callers managing file paths and locking. The split storage format
requires coordinated writes across multiple files (index + task.yaml
+ notes.yaml), which is unsustainable if every caller implements
its own I/O strategy.

What: Create a TaskDataManager class/module that encapsulates:
- listTasks(filters): reads only the index, returns summary records
- getTask(ref): reads index + per-task directory, returns full record
- createTask(input): writes task directory + index entry atomically
- mutateTask(ref, mutation): atomic read-modify-write with locking
- mutateTasks(refs, mutation): batch atomic operation
- deleteTask(ref): removes directory + index entry atomically
- addNote(ref, note): writes only to notes.yaml (no index update)

How: Start by wrapping the existing monolithic file operations behind
this interface. The initial implementation reads/writes the monolithic
file — the split format comes later. This lets us migrate all callers
to the new interface without changing storage format, then swap the
storage backend independently.

The interface must support the existing write buffer system for batch
operations. File locking moves inside the manager — callers no longer
acquire locks directly.

tasks.title: Implement split storage backend
tasks.description:
Create the split storage backend abstraction inside the task data
manager: format detection, directory layout conventions, and the
routing logic that decides which files to read/write for each
operation type. The child tasks (@task-impl-index and
@task-impl-per-task-files) implement the specific read/write
operations for each file type.

Why: All callers now use the task data manager. The internal storage
can change from monolithic file to split directories without any
caller modifications.

What: Implement the storage backend abstraction with:
- Format detection (monolithic vs split) for dual-format support
- Directory layout: .kspec/tasks/<full-ulid>/ per task
- Routing: which operations touch the index, which touch per-task
  files, which touch both
- Per-task file locking replacing whole-file locking

The actual index read/write and per-task file read/write operations
are implemented by the child tasks. This task provides the framework
they plug into.

How: Add a storage backend interface to the task data manager. The
split backend implements format detection (does .kspec/tasks/ exist
with ULID directories?), directory management, and routing logic.
Atomic writes use the existing write buffer — buffer all file writes,
flush as one shadow branch commit.

tasks.title: Implement task index file operations
tasks.description:
Implement the index file read/write operations within the split
storage backend.

Why: The index is what makes list operations fast. Without it,
listing tasks requires scanning every task directory and reading
every task.yaml file.

What: Define which fields are indexed (ulid, slugs, title, status,
priority, type, tags, spec_ref, plan_ref, review_ref, depends_on,
automation, timestamps). Implement index reads for listTasks and
index writes that keep the index in sync with per-task mutations.

How: The index is a standard YAML array in project.tasks.yaml with
the same schema validation as today but fewer fields per entry. On
mutations that affect indexed fields, the manager reads the index,
updates the matching entry, writes it back. On note-only mutations,
the index is untouched. The index write is included in the same
write buffer transaction as the per-task file writes.

tasks.title: Implement per-task core data and notes files
tasks.description:
Implement task.yaml and notes.yaml read/write operations within the
split storage backend.

Why: These are the per-task files that replace the monolithic blob.
task.yaml holds core data plus the append-only history section.
notes.yaml holds the notes array separately to keep task.yaml small.

What: task.yaml contains all current task fields minus notes, plus a
history array. Each history entry has timestamp, author, command,
and a changes object with field names mapped to previous/new values.
notes.yaml contains the notes array in the current schema format.

Note: spec_ref is @task-core-data-file but this task also covers
@task-notes-file ACs (notes.yaml implementation). Both specs must
have AC coverage.

How: On field mutations, update the field in-place and append a
history entry. On note additions, append to notes.yaml only. On
task reads, merge task.yaml fields with notes.yaml notes to produce
the unified task object that callers expect.

notes.author: @claude
notes.content:
Implemented per-task core data and notes files. Key design decisions:

1. History entries are internal to split storage (not in TaskSchema) — stored in task.yaml alongside core fields, stripped on load, returned separately via getTaskHistory().

2. Field diff computation uses JSON.stringify equality for deep comparison, skipping internal fields (notes, todos, history, _sourceFile).

3. Note-only mutations (addNote) skip task.yaml entirely — the split backend detects when no core fields changed and avoids writing task.yaml or creating history entries.

4. MutationMetadata (author/command) is threaded from TaskDataManager.commitOpts through to the backend. When commitOpts is absent, author falls back to getAuthor() and command defaults to 'unknown'.

5. Full AC coverage: 25 tests covering all 3 ACs of @task-core-data-file and all 3 ACs of @task-notes-file. All 6818 tests pass with zero regressions.

tasks.title: Implement in-file activity timeline
tasks.description:
Replace the git log -L based activity extraction with history entries
from task.yaml.

Why: git log -L on the monolithic file takes 35+ seconds for old
tasks. The in-file history provides instant activity timelines.

What: Update getRawTaskCommits and normalizeTaskActivity (or their
replacements) to read history entries from task.yaml instead of
running git log -L. Merge note timestamps from notes.yaml into the
timeline. For tasks migrated from the old format, fall back to
git log -- tasks/<ulid>/ (per-directory git log, which is fast).

How: The activity module reads task.yaml history entries and
notes.yaml timestamps, merges them chronologically, and produces
the same ActivityEntry[] format the CLI and daemon already consume.
The git log -L codepath is removed. A lightweight git log fallback
handles pre-migration tasks that lack history entries.

tasks.title: Extend write buffer for multi-file task transactions
tasks.description:
Extend the existing write buffer system to handle multi-file task
transactions where a single logical operation touches the index,
task.yaml, and notes.yaml.

Why: A status change that also adds a note must update three files
atomically (index + task.yaml + notes.yaml). If any write fails,
none should persist. The existing write buffer handles this for
batch operations but needs to be the default for all task mutations.

What: Ensure that every task mutation — not just batch operations —
uses a write buffer. The manager opens a buffer, queues all file
writes, then flushes as one shadow branch commit. This replaces the
current pattern where single-task mutations write files individually.

How: The task data manager wraps each mutation in a write buffer
scope. For single-task operations this is lightweight (2-3 files).
For batch operations the existing batch write buffer continues to
work — the manager detects when a batch buffer is already active
and uses it instead of creating a nested one.

notes.author: @claude
notes.content: Implemented withWriteBuffer() in TaskDataManager that wraps all task mutations (createTask, mutateTask, mutateTasks, deleteTask) in a write buffer scope. For split format, the manager activates a buffer before calling the backend, and the backend detects it via getActiveBatchBuffer() — reusing it instead of creating a local buffer. For monolithic format, buffer is skipped (single-file writes are atomic under file lock). When a batch buffer is already active, the manager reuses it. Added 12 tests across all 4 ACs covering: single buffer transaction for create/mutate/delete (ac-1), rollback on failure (ac-2), batch buffer reuse (ac-3), multi-task atomic operations (ac-4). Full test suite passes (6831 tests, 0 regressions).

tasks.title: Build index rebuild command
tasks.description:
Build the kspec task rebuild-index command that regenerates
project.tasks.yaml from per-task directories.

Why: If the index drifts from per-task files (bug, manual edit,
interrupted write), users need a repair tool. The index is a derived
cache and must always be rebuildable from authoritative per-task data.

What: A CLI command that scans .kspec/tasks/*/ directories, reads
each task.yaml, extracts indexed fields, and writes a fresh
project.tasks.yaml. Reports differences between the old and new
index. In repair mode (--repair), overwrites the index. Supports
--dry-run to preview without writing.

How: Scan the tasks directory for ULID-named subdirectories. Read
task.yaml from each. Build the index entries. Compare with the
current index and report diffs. On --repair, write the rebuilt index
and commit to shadow branch.

tasks.title: Build migration command
tasks.description:
Build the kspec task migrate command that transforms the monolithic
project.tasks.yaml into the split per-task directory format, and
handles backfilling tasks written in legacy format after migration.

Why: Other users of the project need a supported migration path.
The command also handles backfill: if older tooling or a previous
kspec version writes tasks to the monolithic file after an initial
migration, running migrate again should pick up the new tasks
without affecting existing per-task directories.

What: A CLI command that reads the monolithic file, creates per-task
directories with task.yaml and notes.yaml, rewrites project.tasks.yaml
as a lean index, and commits everything atomically. Supports dry-run
mode. On subsequent runs, detects tasks in the monolithic file that
don't have corresponding per-task directories and backfills them.

How: Read the current monolithic file. For each task: check if a
per-task directory already exists (skip if so). Otherwise extract
notes into notes.yaml, write remaining fields plus an empty history
array into task.yaml, create the directory. Build the index from
the extracted filterable fields. Use the write buffer to collect all
writes, then flush as one shadow branch commit. Dry-run collects
writes but discards instead of flushing.

Edge cases: tasks with validation errors are migrated as-is with
warnings. Tasks with no notes get an empty notes.yaml. Fully
migrated projects with no monolithic tasks report "already migrated."

CRITICAL: Agents working on this task must never use npm run dev,
node dist/, or npm link to run in-progress code against live shadow
branch data. Always use the globally installed kspec binary for CLI
operations. All testing must use the test harness with temp fixtures.

tasks.title: Activate split storage format
tasks.description:
Activate the split storage format after migration has been run and
verified. This is the switchover point — after this, all task writes
go to the split format.

Why: The migration command creates the per-task directories but the
system continues writing to the monolithic format until explicitly
switched. This task is the deliberate switchover after confirming
the migration is correct.

What: Run the activation command to set the storage format to split.
Verify that subsequent task operations (list, get, add, set, note)
read from and write to the per-task directory structure. Confirm
the index stays in sync.

How: Run the activation command. Exercise the full task lifecycle
through CLI and daemon API. Verify shadow branch commits show
per-task file changes rather than monolithic file changes.

MANUAL ONLY: This task requires human coordination. Migration must
be run first, all dispatch/agent work must be paused, and the
switchover must be verified before resuming automated work.

tasks.title: Remove monolithic task file support
tasks.description:
Remove the monolithic task storage backend and add version-gated legacy detection so that upgrading users get clear migration guidance.

Why: Keeping two storage backends increases complexity and testing surface. The split format is stable and all projects are migrated. The monolithic backend serves no purpose, but removing it requires a detection gate so legacy projects get a clear error instead of a crash.

What:
1. Remove MonolithicBackend class, default singleton, and dead yaml.ts functions (saveTask, mutateTaskAtomically, mutateTasksAtomically, deleteTask, writeRawTaskArray). Keep extractRawTaskArray (used by migrate). Keep the backend registry for future extensibility but remove the monolithic registration.
2. Add version-gated legacy detection in resolveTaskDataManager(): when kynetic version is 1.0 and no task_storage.format: split, error with guidance to run kspec task migrate. This is a higher-level gate than ensureMigrated() which stays as a data-integrity safety net in the split backend.
3. Update kspec task migrate: on successful completion, set task_storage.format: split in manifest and bump kynetic version to 1.1. This replaces the separate activate command.
4. Remove kspec task storage activate and kspec task storage status commands. Move storage format check into kspec doctor as a task storage health check.
5. Update kspec init to generate kynetic: 1.1 with task_storage: { format: split }.
6. Keep z.enum(["monolithic", "split"]) in schema for parsing compatibility — reject monolithic at runtime, not parse time.
7. Create one legacy-format test fixture for testing version-gated detection and migration path.
8. Update error messages in ensureMigrated() and rebuild-index that reference monolithic.

How: Delete the monolithic codepaths, add the version gate in resolveTaskDataManager, update migrate to write the manifest, update init template, add doctor check, create legacy test fixture, verify the full test suite passes.

tasks.title: Remove default timeout from dispatch shadow mutation lock
tasks.description:
Why: Dispatch agents run parallel kspec CLI commands (e.g. kspec review comment, kspec review check) that all acquire the shared dispatch shadow mutation file lock. The current default timeout is 5 seconds, inherited from the general-purpose file-lock DEFAULT_TIMEOUT_MS. When one command holds the lock through its read-modify-write + git commit cycle, sibling commands time out and hard-exit, causing dispatch bootstrap failures and review command failures. The spec says mutations should serialize (ac-2), not race — a timeout that kills the waiter contradicts this.

What: Change the dispatch shadow mutation lock to wait indefinitely by default, relying on stale PID detection (process.kill(pid, 0)) as the safety valve for dead lock holders. The KSPEC_SHADOW_MUTATION_LOCK_TIMEOUT_MS env var remains as an explicit operator override.

How: Three targeted changes:

1. src/parser/file-lock.ts — acquireFileLock(): Support no-timeout mode. When timeoutMs is 0 or Infinity, set deadline to Infinity so the retry loop never triggers the timeout throw. The stale lock detection and 50ms retry interval continue to function normally.

2. src/cli/index.ts — maybeAcquireDispatchMutationLock(): Change the default timeout from undefined (which falls through to DEFAULT_TIMEOUT_MS = 5000) to 0 (wait indefinitely). When KSPEC_SHADOW_MUTATION_LOCK_TIMEOUT_MS is set, use that value. The process.exit catch block stays for explicit timeout overrides.

3. src/agent-runtime/workspace.ts — resolveDispatchMutationLockTimeoutMs(): Return 0 instead of undefined when the env var is unset, so daemon-side lock acquisitions via withDispatchShadowMutationLock also wait indefinitely.

Verification: Existing tests for file-lock stale detection and dispatch mutation serialization should continue to pass. Add tests for the no-timeout path (lock acquired after holder releases without hitting a deadline).

notes.author: @claude
notes.content:
## Context

The task storage split plan (@plan-task-storage-split-per-task-directory-architecture) introduced per-task directory storage where each task lives in .kspec/tasks/<ULID>/. The split backend (src/parser/split-backend.ts) reads task.yaml + notes.yaml from these directories when loading full task details.

## Problem

Spec @task-detail-loading ac-2 requires: "Missing per-task directory with existing index entry: manager returns index data with warning (not silent failure)."

Current behavior in split-backend.ts getTask(): when a per-task directory is missing but an index entry exists, the method returns undefined. The task becomes completely unretrievable even though the index still has its summary fields.

## What needs to change

In the split backend's getTask() method (src/parser/split-backend.ts), when loadTaskFromDir() returns undefined for a ULID that exists in the index:
1. Read the index entry for that ULID
2. Construct a partial LoadedTask from the index fields (it will lack notes, description, history)
3. Emit a warning indicating the per-task directory is missing and suggesting rebuild-index or re-migration
4. Return the partial task rather than undefined

## Why

During activation and production use, if a task directory is corrupted or deleted, the task should degrade gracefully to index-only data rather than vanish entirely. Resilience requirement for split storage.

## AC reference

@task-detail-loading ac-2

tasks.title: Fix worktree guard to detect actual shadow branch, not substring match
tasks.closed_reason: Merged to dev via merge commit 6bba94e608f4e0a8d084da3a765b273d62b4bdd4 after review approval. Verified guard now resolves the main project root when invoked from inside the shadow worktree, retains AC coverage for shadow-path detection, and full npm test passed (6981 tests).

notes.author: @claude
notes.content:
## Problem

The worktree guard (src/cli/commands/guard.ts) uses substring matching to detect if a command is running inside the .kspec shadow branch worktree:

```typescript
function isInKspec(command: string, cwd: string | undefined): boolean {
  if (cwd) {
    const normalizedCwd = cwd.replace(/\\/g, "/");
    if (normalizedCwd.includes("/.kspec") || normalizedCwd.endsWith("/.kspec")) {
      return true;
    }
  }
  // ...
}
```

This fires false positives for any path containing "/.kspec" as a substring, including dispatch worktrees under .kspec-worktrees/ (the default dispatch.worktree_root). Agents working in dispatch worktrees get blocked from running git rebase, git fetch, etc. — operations that are legitimate in task worktrees but dangerous in the shadow branch.

## Why this matters

Dispatch agents routinely need to rebase on the integration branch before starting work. The guard blocks this, forcing agents to skip the rebase and work on potentially stale branches. This was observed in production dispatch runs.

## Root cause

The guard hardcodes "/.kspec" as a substring check. Two problems:

1. The shadow directory is configurable — shadow.directory in kspec.config.yaml defaults to ".kspec" but can be changed (src/parser/config.ts, ShadowConfigSchema). If reconfigured, the guard would fail to protect the actual shadow worktree.

2. The substring match is too broad — ".kspec-worktrees/dispatch/task/foo/01ABC123/" contains "/.kspec" and triggers the guard even though it's a normal git worktree, not the shadow branch.

## What needs to change

Replace substring matching in isInKspec() with detection of the actual shadow branch worktree. The guard runs as a kspec CLI command so it has access to the project config.

### Approach

1. Resolve the actual shadow worktree path from config:
   - Load kspec.config.yaml to get shadow.directory (default: ".kspec")
   - Resolve to absolute path from project root
   - Compare cwd against that resolved path (exact prefix match, not substring)

2. If config loading is too expensive for a hot-path hook, cache or use a faster detection:
   - The shadow worktree's .git file contains "gitdir: ../.git/worktrees/-kspec" (or similar)
   - Check if cwd's .git pointer references a kspec-meta worktree
   - This distinguishes shadow worktree from dispatch worktrees definitively

3. The cd-based detection (line 76: command contains "cd .kspec") also needs the same treatment — check against the configured directory name, not hardcoded ".kspec".

### Key files

- src/cli/commands/guard.ts — isInKspec() function (lines 68-80), evaluateWorktreeGuard() (lines 130-163)
- src/parser/config.ts — ShadowConfigSchema (lines 20-47), resolveConfig() (lines 604-630)
- src/parser/shadow.ts — SHADOW_WORKTREE_DIR constant
- tests/guard-worktree.test.ts — existing tests to extend
- .claude/settings.json — hook definition (PreToolUse matcher for Bash)

### Test cases needed

- cwd is the actual shadow worktree (.kspec/) + dangerous command → BLOCK
- cwd is a dispatch worktree (.kspec-worktrees/dispatch/task/foo/) + rebase → ALLOW
- cwd is a dispatch worktree + kspec-meta deletion → still BLOCK (this is checked separately)
- shadow directory reconfigured to custom path → guard uses configured path
- cwd contains ".kspec" as substring but is not the shadow worktree → ALLOW

## Spec reference

@native-guard-commands ac-worktree-guard: "blocks dangerous git operations in .kspec/" — the spec says "in .kspec/", meaning the shadow branch worktree specifically.

notes.content: Fixed substring matching in worktree guard. Both use SHADOW_WORKTREE_DIR constant. tasks.title: Migrate batch buffer scoping from enterWith to AsyncLocalStorage.run()
tasks.description:
## What

Replace `AsyncLocalStorage.enterWith()` with `AsyncLocalStorage.run()` for all batch write buffer scoping. This affects:

1. `activateBatchBuffer()` / `deactivateBatchBuffer()` in `src/cli/batch-write-buffer.ts` — the enterWith-based API
2. `executeAtomic()` in `src/cli/batch-exec.ts` — the sole production caller
3. Tests in `tests/batch-write-buffer.test.ts` and `tests/task-atomic-writes.test.ts` that use the enterWith API

## Why

`enterWith()` permanently mutates the store for the current async execution context. Under Node 22 with vitest's Promise-chain test runner (`withTimeout` + `limitConcurrency` wrappers), `enterWith(undefined)` cleanup does not reliably propagate to subsequent test contexts, causing intermittent CI failures where a WriteBuffer leaks across tests.

More importantly, `enterWith()` violates the concurrent isolation guarantee (ac-9): if two async operations call `enterWith()`, the second clobbers the first's buffer. `_bufferStorage.run(buffer, callback)` scopes the buffer to the callback's async context and automatically reverts when the callback completes — no manual cleanup needed, no cross-context leaks.

`runWithBuffer()` in the same file already uses `.run()` correctly. Only the `activateBatchBuffer`/`deactivateBatchBuffer` pair still uses `enterWith`.

## How

1. Add `runWithBatchBuffer(specDir, fn)` — a new export that wraps `_bufferStorage.run()` with a callback receiving the buffer. The caller owns flush/discard lifecycle (unlike `runWithBuffer` which auto-flushes).

2. Migrate `executeAtomic()` in `batch-exec.ts`: replace `activateBatchBuffer(realSpecDir)` + try/finally `deactivateBatchBuffer()` with `runWithBatchBuffer(realSpecDir, async (buffer) => { ... })`. Move the entire try/finally body inside the callback. Remove the `deactivateBatchBuffer()` call — `.run()` handles scope exit automatically.

3. Migrate tests in `batch-write-buffer.test.ts`: wrap buffer-aware helper tests in `runWithBatchBuffer` instead of activate+afterEach cleanup. Rewrite singleton tests as scoping tests that verify visibility inside `.run()` and null outside.

4. Migrate tests in `task-atomic-writes.test.ts`: two tests simulate batch-exec with `activateBatchBuffer` — wrap in `runWithBatchBuffer` instead. Remove `deactivateBatchBuffer()` from afterEach.

5. Deprecate `activateBatchBuffer`/`deactivateBatchBuffer` — mark as `@deprecated` with guidance to use `runWithBatchBuffer`.

## Verification

- All 3 test shards pass (npm run test:shard1/2/3)
- No remaining callers of `activateBatchBuffer`/`deactivateBatchBuffer` in src/ (only deprecated exports)
- AC annotations: ac-1 (buffer intercepts writes), ac-9 (concurrent isolation)

All 50 batch-related tests pass. Concurrent isolation (ac-9) verified.

tasks.title: Implement active session registry
tasks.description:
Create the session handle registry that maps session_id to a
minimal interface for prompt delivery, state query, and close.

Why: The session_prompt action type needs a way to find and
interact with live sessions without coupling to ACP internals.
The registry is the bridge between the stateless event/action
system and the stateful session lifecycle.

What: A SessionRegistry class with register(id, handle),
unregister(id), get(id), and listActive(). The SessionHandle
interface exposes: sendPrompt(prompt) → Promise, getState() →
idle|prompting|closed, requestClose(reason) → void. The
registry is owned by the dispatch engine and shared with the
action executor via dependency injection.

How: The registry is a Map<string, SessionHandle>. Handles are
created by the invocation runner when a session starts and
removed during teardown. The handle wraps the ACP client but
doesn't expose it — sendPrompt() calls client.prompt()
internally. Thread safety comes from the prompt queue (ac-8/ac-9
of the lifecycle spec).

Covers: @active-session-registry ac-1 through ac-4.

The registry is a Map<string, SessionHandle> with register, unregister, get, listActive, and closeAll methods. closeAll uses best-effort close (continues if one handle throws). Exported from src/agent-runtime/index.ts. 19 tests cover all 4 ACs including edge cases (re-registration, non-existent unregister, error resilience in closeAll). tasks.title: Refactor invocation runner to multi-turn lifecycle
tasks.description:
Replace the linear prompt-then-teardown flow in invocation.ts
with an event-driven turn loop that keeps the session alive
between turns.

Why: The current runInvocation() sends one prompt, then
unconditionally tears down. Every other feature in this plan
depends on sessions staying alive after a turn completes. This
is the core architectural change.

What: After the first prompt returns (stopReason: end_turn),
the session enters idle state instead of proceeding to teardown.
A prompt queue accepts follow-up prompts from any source. The
runner loops: wait for prompt → send → wait for turn completion
→ idle → repeat. The loop exits when a close is requested or the
grace period expires with no queued prompts.

The session handle (from the registry) is the interface other
components use to enqueue prompts. The runner consumes the queue.

How: runInvocation() becomes an async loop instead of a linear
function. The state machine is: spawning → prompting → idle →
(prompting | closing). The idle state emits session.idle on the
event bus (via a callback, same pattern as onInvocationEvent).
A grace period timer starts on each idle entry — if no prompt
arrives before it expires and the session isn't interactive, the
loop breaks and teardown proceeds. The existing timeout_minutes
applies to total session duration, not per-turn.

Backward compatibility: when no hooks target session.idle and

tasks.title: Implement session_prompt action type
tasks.description:
Add the session_prompt action type to the shared action model
and implement its execution in the action executor.

Why: This is the action that makes trigger-driven multi-turn
sessions work. Without it, hooks on session.idle can only spawn
new invocations or run commands — they can't send prompts to the
session that just went idle.

What: Add SessionPromptActionSchema to action.ts with fields:
type ("session_prompt"), prompt (optional), prompt_template
(optional), session_id (optional — defaults to event's
session_id for session.idle hooks). Add to the ActionSchema
discriminated union and ACTION_TYPES constant. Implement
executeSessionPrompt() in ActionExecutor that resolves the
target session from the registry, delivers the prompt via the
session handle, and tracks the action run until the turn
completes.

How: The executor resolves session_id from either the explicit
field or the event context (for session.idle hooks). It calls
registry.get(sessionId) to get the handle, then
handle.sendPrompt(interpolatedPrompt). The action run stays
in running state until the prompt delivery promise resolves
(which happens when the agent's turn completes). If the session
is closed, the action fails with a clear error.

Covers: @session-prompt-action ac-1 through ac-7,
@session-prompt-action-schema ac-1 through ac-4.

Note: @session-prompt-action ac-2 (action lifecycle events) is
inherited from the shared action model pattern — verified by
existing action executor tests.

tasks.title: Implement idle grace period and auto-close logic
tasks.description:
Implement the grace period that determines when an idle session
auto-closes, and the session mode flag that can disable it.

Why: Backward compatibility requires that sessions without
idle-targeting hooks close automatically after one turn, matching
current behavior. Sessions with hooks or a non-auto-close mode
need to stay open. The grace period bridges these modes.

What: When a session enters idle, a configurable timer starts
(default 5 seconds). If no prompt arrives before it expires and
the session mode allows auto-close, the session closes. The
timer resets if a prompt is queued. The agent definition schema
gets a session mode field and an idle timeout field.

How: The grace period timer is part of the turn loop in
invocation.ts. It races against the prompt queue — whichever
fires first wins. For auto-close mode, the grace period is short
(enough for hooks to fire and queue prompts). For modes that
disable auto-close, only idle timeout applies. The agent schema
extension is in meta.ts.

Covers: @multi-turn-session-lifecycle ac-5, ac-6, ac-7, ac-11.

tasks.title: Integrate multi-turn lifecycle with dispatch engine
tasks.description:
Wire the multi-turn invocation lifecycle into the dispatch
engine, ensuring session registry, event emission, concurrency
tracking, and post-invocation cleanup all work with sessions
that span multiple turns.

Why: The dispatch engine currently assumes runInvocation() = one
prompt = done. With multi-turn sessions, a single runInvocation()
call may span many turns over a longer duration. Concurrency
tracking, task exclusivity, timeout enforcement, and event
emission all need to account for this.

What: The dispatch engine registers sessions in the registry
before spawning. It receives session.idle events from the bus
(for metrics/logging). The per-task exclusivity lock is held for
the entire multi-turn session, not released after each turn.
The overall timeout_minutes still applies to the total session
duration. invocation.completed fires once when the session
finally closes, with turn_count in the payload.

How: _spawnInvocation() registers the session handle before
calling runInvocation(). The onIdle callback (from the invocation
runner) emits session.idle on the event bus. Post-invocation
cleanup runs when runInvocation() returns (after the turn loop
exits and teardown completes). The existing invocation.completed
event payload is extended with turn_count.

Covers: @multi-turn-session-lifecycle ac-1, ac-2, ac-3, ac-4
(integration-level verification of state machine wired through
dispatch), ac-12, ac-13, ac-14.

tasks.title: Add skill support to session_prompt actions
tasks.description:
## What

Session prompt actions (used by hooks to deliver follow-up prompts to idle sessions) currently only support literal text and template variable interpolation. They cannot include skill content or resolve cross-skill references. This means follow-up turns (e.g. a reflection prompt after a worker completes a turn) get a raw text prompt with no access to skill instructions that the initial invocation prompt receives automatically.

## Why

The multi-turn session lifecycle enables hooks on session.idle to inject prompts into a live session. A key use case is sending a reflection skill prompt to a task worker after their turn completes. Without skill support, the prompt is just plain text — it cannot leverage the structured guidance that skills provide. The initial invocation prompt already resolves skills via buildPromptWithSkills() (AC: @agent-invocation-lifecycle ac-7, ac-10), but session_prompt actions bypass that entirely.

## How

Three changes, all scoped to the session_prompt action path:

### 1. Schema — @session-prompt-action-schema ac-5
Add an optional `skills` field to SessionPromptActionBaseSchema in src/schema/action.ts:
- `skills: z.array(z.string()).optional()`
- Follows the same pattern as agent definition `skills` field
- Existing actions without skills continue to work unchanged

### 2. Skill content resolution — @session-prompt-action ac-8
In ActionExecutor.executeSessionPrompt() (src/agent-runtime/action-executor.ts), after resolving the prompt text via resolveTemplateVars(), call buildPromptWithSkills() when action.skills is non-empty:
- `buildPromptWithSkills({ basePrompt: resolvedPrompt, skillIds: action.skills, specDir, adapterId })`
- specDir: derivable from projectDir (already available on ActionExecutor) via initContext()
- adapterId: needs to be resolved from the session's agent definition. The session.idle event payload includes agent_id — look up the agent to get its adapter. Options:
  - Add adapter_id to ActionEventContext (populated by dispatch when emitting session.idle)
  - Or look up agent definition from meta context using agent_id from event context
- buildPromptWithSkills already handles empty skill lists (returns basePrompt unchanged) so the no-skills path is a no-op

### 3. Skill reference rewriting — @session-prompt-action ac-9
buildPromptWithSkills() already calls rewriteSkillReferencesForAdapter() as its final step, so {skill:foo} tokens in both the prompt template and injected skill content are rewritten to adapter-appropriate invocation format (/foo for Claude Code, $foo for Codex, etc.). This comes free from using the existing code path.

### Key files
- src/schema/action.ts — SessionPromptActionBaseSchema
- src/agent-runtime/action-executor.ts — executeSessionPrompt()
- src/agent-runtime/prompts.ts — buildPromptWithSkills() (already exists, reuse as-is)

### Testing
- Unit test: action-executor executeSessionPrompt with skills list resolves skill content
- Unit test: schema validates skills field (present, absent, empty array)
- Unit test: skill references in injected content are rewritten for adapter
- Integration test: hook on session.idle with session_prompt action + skills delivers skill-enriched prompt to session

tasks.title: Expand kspec meta set agent with missing schema fields
tasks.description:
## What

`kspec meta set` for agents is missing CLI flags for fields that exist on the `AgentSchema`. The current command covers name, description, adapter, auto_approve, capabilities/tools/conventions/skills (add only), dispatch rules (add/remove/clear), and budget/concurrency scalars — but not session config, prompt_template, automation, tags, array removal, initial_response_timeout_seconds, or session clearing.

## Why

The multi-turn session lifecycle added `session.mode`, `session.idle_grace_period_ms`, and `session.idle_timeout_ms` to agent definitions, but these can only be set via manual YAML editing. The reflection hooks we've configured need session config (e.g. persistent mode, custom grace periods) to be tunable per-agent. Beyond session config, other schema fields have accumulated without corresponding CLI flags, creating an expanding gap between what the schema supports and what the CLI exposes.

## How

All changes are in `src/cli/commands/meta-crud.ts` (the `meta set` command handler) and `src/parser/meta.ts` (the `updateMetaItem` function that persists changes).

### 1. Session config flags — @agent-definition-schema ac-13
Add three flags to the `meta set` command:
- `--session-mode <mode>` — validates against SessionModeSchema (auto_close | persistent)
- `--idle-grace-period-ms <n>` — non-negative integer
- `--idle-timeout-ms <n>` — positive integer

These merge into the existing `session` object on the agent, preserving fields not specified. If the agent has no session config yet, a new session object is created with only the specified fields.

### 2. Clear session — @agent-definition-schema ac-14
- `--clear-session` — removes the `session` key entirely from the agent definition, reverting to runtime defaults (dispatch engine auto-detects grace period from hook presence)

### 3. Additional scalar/enum fields — @agent-definition-schema ac-15
- `--prompt-template <text>` — string, sets `prompt_template`
- `--automation <status>` — validates against enum (eligible | ineligible)
- `--initial-response-timeout-seconds <n>` — positive integer, sets `budget.initial_response_timeout_seconds` (merges into existing budget object like other budget flags)

### 4. Array removal and tag operations — @agent-definition-schema ac-16
Add `--remove-*` variants for existing add-only arrays:
- `--remove-capability <cap>`
- `--remove-tool <tool>`
- `--remove-convention <conv>`
- `--remove-skill <skill>`

Add tag operations (new array field, not currently exposed):
- `--add-tag <tag>`
- `--remove-tag <tag>`

Remove operations should fail gracefully if the item isn't in the array (no-op with a warning, not an error).

### Key files
- `src/cli/commands/meta-crud.ts` — command flag definitions and handler logic
- `src/parser/meta.ts` — updateMetaItem() persistence logic
- `tests/meta-crud.test.ts` — existing test file for meta CRUD

### Testing
- Per-flag tests: each new flag updates the correct field and preserves others
- Session merge: setting one session field preserves others already set
- Clear session: removes session object entirely
- Remove from array: item removed; removing non-existent item is a no-op
- Tag add/remove: works like other array fields
- Validation: invalid enum values, negative numbers, etc. produce clear errors
- Batch support: verify new flags work via kspec batch with meta set command

tasks.title: Fix web UI pages not rendering on initial load
tasks.description:
## Problem

The dashboard, agents, and automation pages in the web UI do not render their content on initial page load. The pages show loading skeletons or empty states indefinitely, even though network requests complete without errors. Navigating away to a different page and then back causes the content to appear correctly (served from TanStack Query cache).

The same issue affects settings, sessions/[id], and tasks/board — any page where a TanStack Query `enabled` condition includes `!isStaticMode()`.

## Root Cause

Pages that work (tasks, triage, inbox) gate their queries with only `enabled: isProjectInitialized()`. Pages that break additionally include `!isStaticMode()`, which reads the `mode` $state variable from the mode store.

TanStack Query v6 for Svelte 5 uses an internal `$effect` to subscribe to query observer state changes. When components are created inside the layout's conditional render gate (`{#if ready}`), this `$effect` does not reliably fire (known upstream issue: TanStack/query PR #9810). The extra reactive dependency on `mode` exacerbates this — queries with a single `$state` dependency (`initialized`) work, while queries with two (`initialized` + `mode`) do not.

When the subscription `$effect` fails to fire, the query fetches data but the proxy object backing the query result never updates. The component stays in its initial loading state until remount (navigation away and back), at which point cached data is available immediately and the initial render succeeds.

## Fix

Move static mode guards from query `enabled` conditions into the API fetch functions. This matches the pattern already used by `fetchTasks`, `fetchInbox`, `fetchPlans`, and other functions that check `isStaticMode()` internally and return snapshot data.

Daemon-only fetch functions that currently lack static mode handling need guards added: `fetchAgentStatus`, `fetchAgentDefinitions`, `fetchHooks`, `fetchSchedules`, `fetchScheduleStatus`, `fetchRecentEvents`, `fetchHealth`, `fetchShadowStatus`, `fetchCompositionConfigs`, `fetchCompositionActivations`.

After adding API-layer guards, remove `&& !isStaticMode()` from all query `enabled` conditions across pages and components, leaving only `enabled: isProjectInitialized()`.

This satisfies @ui-data-freshness ac-6 (no daemon HTTP calls in static mode) and @gh-pages-export ac-25 (all views with snapshot data render without a daemon connection) while eliminating the problematic dual-$state dependency.

## Scope

- 1 API file: add static mode fallbacks to ~10 daemon-only fetch functions
- 8 page/component files: simplify query `enabled` to `isProjectInitialized()` only
- 1 test file: update 3 assertions that check for `!isStaticMode()` in page source

notes.author: @claude
notes.content:
Implementation plan:

1. Create tools/eslint-rules/no-source-scanning.js — ESM plugin with a single rule
2. Four-phase AST detection:
   - Phase 1: Track fs imports (readFileSync/readFile from fs/node:fs/node:fs/promises)
   - Phase 2: Track source-path variables (paths containing src/, templates/, packages/*/src/)
   - Phase 3: Detect read calls where arg resolves to a source path (direct or via variable)
   - Phase 4: Track read result variables and flag assertions on them (expect().toContain/toMatch, .includes, .match)
3. Register in .oxlintrc.json test file overrides via jsPlugins
4. Verify it catches known offending tests
5. Verify it does NOT flag legitimate tests (reading fixtures, temp dirs, generated output)

Key constraint: oxlint JS Plugin runtime is sandboxed — no Node.js built-ins. Pure AST analysis only.

notes.author: @claude
notes.content:
Rule implemented and tested. Coverage:
- 9 of 12 offending files caught (466+ violations detected)
- 1 file correctly excluded (web-ui-design-system reads build output, not source)
- 2 edge cases missed: daemon-api-input-validation (for-of destructuring over inline array of source paths) and daemon-executable (dynamic import('fs/promises'))
- 0 false positives on legitimate test files (integration, module, meta, etc.)

Patterns detected: ESM imports, require() destructuring, direct paths, path.join/resolve calls, variable indirection through sourcePathVars, expect().toContain/toMatch assertions, string .includes()/.match() calls.

The 2 missed edge cases are niche — dynamic import() and array destructuring iteration. These can be added later if needed but the rule catches the vast majority of the anti-pattern.

notes.author: @claude
notes.content:
Final state: rule detects 477+ violations in known offending files with 0 false positives. Created readTestOutput/readTestOutputSync helpers in tests/helpers/cli.ts. Converted 29 test files + 1 example (claude-code-renderer) to use the helper. The only remaining detection outside known offending files is cli-version.test.ts which reads package.json — a legitimate detection.

One edge case still missed: daemon-executable.test.ts uses dynamic import('fs/promises') which the rule can't detect. This file is already tracked for deletion in the static analysis cleanup plan.

tasks.title: Fix split backend mutex: hold lock through write flush
tasks.description:
Why: The split backend's per-task mutex releases the lock before runWithBuffer flushes writes to disk. This creates a TOCTOU race: concurrent mutations on the same task read stale state because the previous mutation's write hasn't flushed yet. The last writer wins and earlier mutations are silently lost. This violates @task-data-manager ac-9 (concurrent same-task mutations must serialize without data corruption) and ac-10 (delete + mutate must fully complete before the other begins).

7 tests are currently skipped with TODO comments citing this bug:
- tests/task-data-manager.test.ts lines 757, 798, 838, 886 (4 tests)
- tests/task-mutation-serialization.test.ts lines 63, 99 (2 tests)
These tests verify concurrent mutations preserve all state changes and notes.

What: In src/parser/split-backend.ts, the SplitBackend.mutateTask method (around line 722) acquires the per-task lock via this.taskMutex.acquire(), then releases it in a try/finally block that wraps only the mutation logic. The runWithBuffer flush happens after lock release. The fix is to hold the lock through the entire operation including the write flush. The same pattern needs to be checked and fixed in mutateTasks and deleteTask methods.

Specifically:
1. Move releaseTaskLock() in mutateTask to AFTER runWithBuffer completes (not in the inner try/finally)
2. Apply the same fix to deleteTask — hold lock through the buffer flush
3. Verify mutateTasks acquires locks for all target ULIDs and holds them through flush
4. Unskip all 7 tests listed above (remove the .skip and TODO comments)
5. Run the full test suite to verify no deadlocks or regressions from holding locks longer

How: The fix is small — restructure the try/finally in mutateTask, deleteTask, and potentially mutateTasks so that the lock release happens after the buffer flush, not before. The key insight is that the lock must protect the entire read-mutate-write cycle, not just read-mutate.
tasks.closed_reason: Merged to dev. Per-task mutex moved from SplitBackend to TaskDataManager to hold lock through buffer flush, fixing TOCTOU race on concurrent same-task mutations. 6 previously-skipped tests now active and passing. All prior review findings addressed across 3 cycles.

notes.author: @claude
notes.content:
Approach: The bug is that SplitBackend.mutateTask/mutateTasks/deleteTask acquire per-task locks, but when called through TaskDataManager.withWriteBuffer, the buffer flush happens AFTER the backend method returns (and lock is released). Each concurrent TaskDataManager.mutateTask creates its own isolated buffer via AsyncLocalStorage.run(), so concurrent callers cannot see each other's buffered writes. This creates a TOCTOU race: Mutation B reads stale disk state after Mutation A has buffered writes but before A's buffer flushes.

Fix plan:
1. Remove per-task locking from SplitBackend.mutateTask, mutateTasks, deleteTask
2. Remove SplitBackend's internal runWithBuffer calls (TaskDataManager.withWriteBuffer already provides the buffer)
3. Add per-task lock acquisition in TaskDataManager.mutateTask, mutateTasks, deleteTask wrapping withWriteBuffer (only for split backend, monolithic already has its own file-level locking)
4. This ensures the lock spans read → mutate → buffer-write → flush
5. Unskip all 7 tests and verify they pass

notes.author: @claude
notes.content:

When called through TaskDataManager.withWriteBuffer, each concurrent mutation got its own isolated buffer (via AsyncLocalStorage.run), and the SplitBackend released the lock before the outer buffer flushed. This created a TOCTOU race: a second mutation would read stale disk state while the first mutation's writes were still in its buffer.

Fix: Moved per-task lock from SplitBackend to TaskDataManager, wrapping withWriteBuffer so the lock spans read → mutate → buffer → flush. Removed the now-redundant SplitTaskMutexMap class from split-backend.ts.

tasks.title: Preserve unknown fields through split backend mutateTask writes
tasks.description:
Why: The split backend's writeTaskFile writes schema-validated data that has been through TaskSchema.safeParse(), which strips unknown fields by default (Zod behavior). The monolithic backend avoided this by using mergeTaskPreservingRawShape() to overlay validated data onto the raw YAML, keeping custom fields intact. The split backend never does this merge — it writes coreDataAfter directly, losing any fields not in the schema.

This means external tooling or future extensions that store custom fields in task.yaml (e.g. crm_id, backend_metadata) would silently lose those fields on the next kspec mutation. This violates @task-core-data-file ac-4 (unknown fields preserved through mutations) and is related to @task-directory-storage ac-3 (unknown files/dirs preserved).

1 test is currently skipped citing this bug:
- tests/task-data-manager.test.ts line 1234: "preserves unknown fields through mutateTask"

What:
1. In src/parser/split-backend.ts, the mutateTask method loads the task via TaskSchema.safeParse() which drops unknown fields. Before writing, it needs to merge the mutated data back onto the raw file contents to preserve unknown fields.
2. Read the raw YAML from the task file before parsing, keep it as the base. After mutation, merge the schema-validated result onto the raw data (same pattern as mergeTaskPreservingRawShape in yaml.ts).
3. Unskip the test at line 1234 in task-data-manager.test.ts.
4. Run the full test suite to verify no regressions.

How: The approach mirrors what the monolithic backend did. In mutateTask, after getting the mutated task:
- Read the raw YAML from the task file (or keep it from the initial load)
- Use mergeTaskPreservingRawShape (or equivalent logic) to overlay schema-known fields from the mutation result onto the raw data
- Write the merged result via writeTaskFile
The key is that unknown fields from the raw file survive the round-trip.

tasks.title: Smart error message for task set --status rejection
tasks.description:
## What

When a user runs `kspec task set @ref --status <target>`, the CLI rejects the command because status changes must go through dedicated transition commands. Currently the error message is generic: "Use state transition commands (start, complete, block, etc.) to change status". It doesn't mention the task's current state, doesn't suggest the specific command needed, and doesn't even list all transition commands (omits needs-work, submit, unblock).

## Why

Agents and users who don't know the exact transition command names get stuck. The generic error provides no actionable path forward — the user has to guess or search docs for the right command. This caused an automated agent to ignore the error entirely and use the wrong fallback (blocking a task instead of transitioning to needs_work). A context-aware error message would have prevented the mistake.

## How

In `src/cli/commands/task.ts` at the `--status` rejection point (~line 1302):

1. Load the task to get its current status
2. Map the requested target status to the correct transition command name and required flags (e.g. needs_work → `kspec task needs-work @ref --reason "..."`, in_progress → `kspec task start @ref`)
3. Build an error message that includes:
   - The task's current status
   - If the requested transition is valid: the exact command to use
   - If the requested transition is invalid: why it's invalid and what transitions ARE valid from current state
4. Ensure the error satisfies @trait-error-guidance ac-4 (current state + valid next states) and @spec-task-set-batch ac-3 (specific command for requested status)

The transition command mapping:
- pending/needs_work → `kspec task start @ref`
- in_progress → `kspec task submit @ref`  
- pending_review → `kspec task complete @ref --reason "..."` or `kspec task needs-work @ref --reason "..."`
- blocked → `kspec task block @ref --reason "..."`
- completed → `kspec task complete @ref --reason "..."`
- cancelled → `kspec task cancel @ref`

Error strings live in `src/strings/errors.ts`.

tasks.title: Blocked Review
Implement entity cache with tiered storage and watcher invalidation
tasks.description:
Build the entity cache with two-tier storage (index hot, detail on
demand) and wire it to the existing file watcher for invalidation.
Integrate with the project registration lifecycle.

Why: The daemon currently re-reads all YAML files and rebuilds indexes
on every API request. initContext() + loadAllItems() + loadAllTasks()
runs on every route handler. The entity cache eliminates this by
loading index data once on project registration and serving from
memory, with the file watcher driving selective reloads on change.

What:
- Implement ProjectEntityCache class with per-domain storage. Each
  domain has an index tier (always hot) and a detail tier (loaded on
  demand, evicted on invalidation). See the cache tiering table in
  Implementation Notes for what goes where per domain.
- Wire to file watcher in packages/daemon/src/watcher.ts — add cache
  invalidation alongside the existing WebSocket broadcast. Map changed
  file paths to domains using the domain mapping table (see
  Implementation Notes).
- Implement reload dedup using in-flight promise dedup (Map<domain,
  Promise>) — proven pattern from shadowPull(). Multiple file changes
  within the watcher's existing 500ms debounce window produce a single
  reload per affected domain.
- Implement write-through: daemon API write routes update the cache
  before returning. Use a write-through flag that causes the watcher
  callback to skip the redundant reload for that domain.
- Implement graceful degradation: if cache load fails for a domain,
  mark the domain as degraded, fall back to direct file reading for
  requests to that domain, and log the error.
- Implement progressive loading: on project registration, load
  domains in priority order (tasks → items → meta → inbox → plans →
  triage → reviews → sessions). Serve loaded domains from cache
  immediately; unloaded domains return a loading indicator.
- Implement session index bounding: cache only the N most recent
  session summaries (configurable, default 100). Apply stale session
  exclusion: sessions with active status that exceed the existing
  stale criteria (older-than + inactive-for thresholds from
  @session-stale-criteria) are not treated as active in the index.
  Sessions outside the window are loaded on demand when accessed by
  ID.
- Implement project isolation: each registered project gets its own
  ProjectEntityCache instance. Watcher events are scoped to the
  project whose files changed.
- On project unregister: release all cached data and cancel any
  in-flight reloads.
- Absorb the existing SessionSummaryCache (src/sessions/cache.ts)
  into the unified cache — the session domain replaces the standalone
  session cache.

How: The cache lives in packages/daemon/ alongside project-context.ts.
ProjectContextManager.registerProject() creates the cache instance
and starts the initial load. The watcher callback in
packages/daemon/src/watcher.ts gets a second handler (alongside the
existing WebSocket broadcast) that maps file paths to domains and
calls cache.invalidateDomain(). Build the domain mapping from the
same file patterns used by the existing YAML loading functions.

For tasks: TaskDataManager already has listTasks() returning
TaskSummary[] and rawToSummary() — use this as the index tier. Full
task detail (notes, todos) loaded via getTask() on demand.

For items: No ItemSummary type exists yet. Create one with the index
fields (ulid, title, type, status, priority, tags, traits, parent
path). Full item detail (ACs, description, notes) loaded on demand.

For sessions: Reuse the existing stale criteria resolution from
src/sessions/store.ts (resolveStaleSessionCriteria) to determine
whether an active-status session should be treated as stale in the
cache index.

Covers: @daemon-entity-cache ac-load-on-register, ac-serve-from-memory,
ac-detail-on-demand, ac-watcher-invalidation, ac-granular-reload,
ac-write-through, ac-concurrent-reads, ac-reload-dedup,
ac-graceful-degradation, ac-project-isolation, ac-unregister-cleanup,
ac-session-bounded-index, ac-session-stale-exclusion,
ac-warming-availability, ac-progressive-loading.
tasks.closed_reason: Merged to dev after review approval. writeThrough() now only sets watcher-skip when reload leaves the domain ready, and regression coverage now proves failed writeThrough reloads degrade without suppressing the next watcher recovery invalidation.

notes.author: @claude
notes.content:
Approach: Implement ProjectEntityCache in packages/daemon/src/entity-cache.ts

Architecture:
- 8 data domains: tasks, items, meta, inbox, plans, triage, reviews, sessions
- Each domain has index tier (always hot) + detail tier (loaded on demand, evicted on invalidation)
- Domain state: loading | ready | degraded | unloaded
- Progressive loading in priority order: tasks → items → meta → inbox → plans → triage → reviews → sessions

Key patterns:
- Reuse TaskDataManager.listTasks()/rawToSummary() for task index tier
- Reuse loadAllItems() for item index (create ItemSummary projection)
- Reuse existing SessionSummaryCache patterns for session domain
- In-flight promise dedup (Map<domain, Promise>) for reload coalescing — proven in SessionSummaryCache.buildPromise
- Write-through flag with domain-level skip to prevent redundant watcher reload
- File path → domain mapping based on existing patterns (project.tasks.yaml → tasks, modules/*.yaml → items, etc.)
- Graceful degradation: domain-level error tracking, fallback to direct file reading per request

Integration points:
- ProjectContextManager.registerProject() creates cache + triggers initial load
- ProjectContextManager.unregisterProject() releases cache + cancels in-flight reloads
- KspecWatcher.onFileChange callback gets cache invalidation handler alongside existing pubsub + dispatch
- Route handlers check cache before falling back to disk reads (backward compatible)

Session bounding:
- Reuse resolveStaleSessionCriteria() for stale exclusion
- Configurable retention window (default 100 most recent)
- Sessions outside window accessible on demand

Absorbing SessionSummaryCache:
- The session domain in ProjectEntityCache replaces the standalone SessionSummaryCache
- Existing getSessionCache() registry pattern replaced by per-project cache instance
- Live event counters migrate to session domain

Test plan: 15 ACs × behavioral E2E/integration tests each. Tests will create temp fixtures, register mock projects, and verify cache behavior through the public API.

tasks.title: Migrate daemon read routes to serve from entity cache
tasks.description:
Update all daemon API read routes to serve from the entity cache
instead of calling initContext() + loadAll* per request. Move
per-request drift-check to the background sync scheduler.

Why: The cache exists but routes still bypass it. This task connects
routes to the cache and eliminates per-request filesystem I/O and
git operations. This is where the user-visible performance improvement
actually happens.

What:
- Replace initContext() + loadAllItems/loadAllTasks/loadPlans calls
  in every read route with cache lookups. Affected route files in
  packages/daemon/src/routes/: tasks.ts, items.ts, inbox.ts,
  plans.ts, triage.ts, reviews.ts, meta.ts, sessions.ts,
  aggregation.ts, validation.ts (includes search handling), refs.ts
- List routes use the index tier; detail routes (GET by ref) use
  the detail tier (on-demand load if not cached)
- Build ReferenceIndex and AlignmentIndex from cached index data
  rather than fresh disk reads
- Move drift-check sync from per-request to background scheduler:
  the existing ShadowSyncScheduler in shadow-sync.ts already runs
  periodically — extend it to invalidate the entity cache when new
  data is pulled
- Ensure write routes still apply mutations through the normal
  shadow branch commit path, using write-through to update the cache
- Ensure API response payloads remain identical — field names,
  nesting, ordering must not change from the migration
- Batch endpoints (e.g. @batch-item-fetch-api) also serve from cache

How: Each route currently does:
  const ctx = await initContext(projectPath);
  const items = await loadAllItems(ctx);
Replace with:
  const cache = getProjectCache(projectPath);
  const items = cache.getItemIndex();  // hot index tier
For detail routes:
  const item = await cache.getItemDetail(ref);  // on-demand
Background sync: add a post-pull hook to the existing
ShadowSyncScheduler that calls cache.invalidate() when shadowPull()
returns changes.

Covers: @daemon-read-path ac-no-per-request-sync, ac-background-sync,
ac-index-from-cache, ac-write-routes-sync.

notes.content:
Approach: Most read routes already have cache-first pattern from @task-entity-cache-impl. Remaining work:

1. meta.ts: Migrate /session, /config, /shadow to cache (session/config can use cached MetaContext; /shadow needs initContext for getShadowStatus which does git operations - will keep disk access but note it's not a read-only data path)
2. aggregation.ts: Wire to cache - /tasks/summary from task index, /validation uses validate() which needs ctx (keep but note validation is computational), /inbox from cached inbox+triage indexes
3. validation.ts: Wire /search to cache for items/tasks/inbox/meta; /validate and /alignment need buildIndexes/validate which are computational
4. Background sync: Wire ShadowSyncScheduler post-pull to invalidate entity cache when new data pulled
5. Build ReferenceIndex/AlignmentIndex from cached data in aggregation and validation routes

Key insight: /validate and /alignment call validate() and buildIndexes() which do deep validation requiring full disk access. These are computational endpoints, not simple data reads - they'll still need initContext but can use cached entity data for index building.

Edge cases: concurrent invalidation during sync, stale cache during watcher gap, /shadow route genuinely needs git operations (not a pure read route for AC purposes).

Test plan: 4 ACs × 1+ behavioral tests each, covering cache-served reads, background sync invalidation, index-from-cache, and write-through.

tasks.title: Implement daemon command API endpoint
tasks.description:
Build the REST endpoint that accepts CLI command payloads and executes
them within the daemon process, returning structured results.

Why: For the CLI to proxy through the daemon, the daemon needs an
endpoint that can execute arbitrary kspec commands. Without it, CLI
mutations would still write directly to the shadow branch, creating
a window of stale data in the daemon's cache.

What:
- POST /api/command endpoint that accepts a command payload using
  the same JSON format as kspec batch command objects (command path
  string + args object)
- Execute the command within the daemon process using Commander's
  parseAsync with captured output streams — avoids child process
  overhead and keeps everything in the daemon's event loop
- Capture stdout, stderr, and exit code; return as structured JSON
- For mutating commands: serialize execution using the dispatch
  mutation lock pattern (acquireFileLock) to prevent concurrent
  shadow branch conflicts
- After successful mutation: update entity cache (write-through)
  before returning the response, broadcast WebSocket event
- Support batch payloads: accept an array of commands, execute
  atomically via the existing batch runner (src/cli/batch.ts),
  update cache once after the batch completes
- Response parity: stdout/stderr content must match what direct CLI
  execution would produce

How: Follow the pattern in packages/daemon/src/routes/agent-dispatch.ts
for route structure and middleware. The command executor wraps
Commander's parseAsync, redirecting process.stdout/stderr to buffers.
Mutation serialization uses the same lock mechanism as the dispatch
engine. Batch execution reuses the existing batch runner. Cache
update happens after the commit but before the HTTP response.

Covers: @daemon-command-api ac-command-endpoint, ac-mutation-cache-update,
ac-batch-support, ac-concurrent-mutations, ac-response-parity.
tasks.closed_reason: Approved review @01KMRG73 after verifying daemon command API behavior, AC annotations, kspec validation status, and full npm test pass. Merged dispatch/task/task-daemon-command-api/01kmmb3v into dev at f3fb67c100a1c342dcbe251b36da3bfa3e6f2112.

notes.author: @claude
notes.content:
Approach: Reusing existing batch infrastructure for command execution.

Implementation plan:
1. Command executor: Reuse OutputCapture + BatchExitError + resetCommandTree from batch-context.ts and batch-exec.ts. Import the Commander program from cli/index.ts. Capture stdout/stderr separately (extend OutputCapture to track stdout vs stderr). The command executes via program.parseAsync() with captured output streams.

2. POST /api/command route: New route file packages/daemon/src/routes/command.ts following the pattern in tasks.ts. Accepts {command: string, args: object} body matching batch schema. For single commands: build argv via buildCommandArgv, execute via parseAsync with output capture.

3. Mutation serialization (ac-concurrent-mutations): Use withFileLock from parser/file-lock.ts. The lock file path will be derived from the project's shadow branch directory. Detect mutating commands using the same command-annotations introspection that batch uses.

4. Cache update + WebSocket broadcast (ac-mutation-cache-update): After successful mutating command, call cache.writeThrough() for all domains that might have changed. Broadcast 'command:executed' event on pubsub.

5. Batch support (ac-batch-support): Accept array of commands, delegate to the existing executeBatch function from batch-exec.ts. Cache update once after batch completes.

6. Response parity (ac-response-parity): Same stdout/stderr captured via OutputCapture that batch uses. Return structured {stdout, stderr, exitCode} matching what CLI would produce.

Edge cases:
- Concurrent mutations: file lock serialization prevents conflicts
- Batch atomicity: reuses existing batch-exec atomic mode
- Non-mutating commands: no lock needed, just execute and return
- Command not found: return 404 with suggestions (reuse batch validation)

Test plan: 5 spec ACs + 6 trait-api-endpoint ACs + 3 trait-localhost-security ACs. E2E tests preferred using HTTP client against daemon.

notes.author: @claude
notes.content:
Implementation complete. Created:
- packages/daemon/src/routes/command.ts — POST /api/command and POST /api/command/batch endpoints
- tests/daemon-command-api.test.ts — 14 tests covering all 5 spec ACs and relevant trait ACs

Key design decisions:
1. Reused existing batch infrastructure (OutputCapture, exit interceptor, buildCommandArgv, resetCommandTree) to avoid reimplementing command dispatch. This ensures response parity (ac-response-parity) because the same capture mechanism is used.
2. withProjectDir() temporarily changes process.cwd() to project path so CLI commands resolve the correct kspec project context.
3. Mutation detection uses the same introspection mechanism as batch command validation (CommandMeta.mutating) — no separate classification needed.
4. File lock path is per-project (.kspec/shadow-mutation) matching the dispatch engine pattern.
5. Write-through covers all mutation-affected domains (tasks, items, meta, inbox, plans, triage, reviews) because commands can have cross-domain side effects.
6. Split backend registered lazily on first getProgram() call since CLI task commands require it.

All 6959 tests pass (5 pre-existing skips). No regressions.
