tasks.description:
## Task 5 — Fix guardrail cleanup-binding and approved-helper analysis

Proposed slug: `task-fix-guardrail-binding-wrapper-analysis`
Type: `task`
Priority: `P2`
Plan ref: `@plan-daemon-test-fixture-hardening`
Spec ref: `@daemon-test-guardrail-precision`
Tags: `daemon-tests`, `lint`, `guardrails`, `follow-up`
Depends on: `@task-add-guardrail-binding-wrapper-regressions`
Automation: leave unassessed until Jacob approves.

### Description

#### What
Fix the `no-leaky-test-daemon` guardrail implementation so it catches the false negatives covered by `@task-add-guardrail-binding-wrapper-regressions` while preserving the existing safe cases.

Target implementation file:

- `tools/eslint-rules/no-leaky-test-daemon.js`

Expected behavior:

- A cleanup callback counts as cleanup for a detached daemon only when the callback owns the concrete pid, child handle, or stop handle for the daemon that was just started before later awaits/assertions/daemon observations can run.
- A cleanup callback that closes over a `let`/mutable variable assigned only after an intervening observation does not satisfy the cleanup-before-observation requirement.
- Local helper functions inside arbitrary test files do not hide unsafe detached starts or direct daemon entrypoint invocations.
- Approved helper exceptions remain explicit and narrow to shared daemon-test fixture utilities and documented guardrail internals.
- Unrelated subprocesses that merely contain words like `serve`, `start`, or `daemon` remain unreported.

#### Why
The existing lint guardrail improved daemon test hygiene but still accepts patterns that can leak detached daemons or bypass shared fixtures. If workers can silence the rule by registering an unbound cleanup closure or by wrapping daemon startup in an arbitrary helper, the repository returns to whackamole: unsafe tests can look superficially compliant while still leaking processes under failure conditions.

#### How
1. Start from the regression tests in `@task-add-guardrail-binding-wrapper-regressions`.
2. Inspect the current rule implementation in `tools/eslint-rules/no-leaky-test-daemon.js`, especially:
   - daemon command detection;
   - cleanup registration detection;
   - observation ordering analysis;
   - approved helper exemptions;
   - suppression/localized-disable checks.
3. Tighten cleanup analysis so safe recognition requires a concrete owned value before observation. For common patterns:
   - allow `const pid = readPidFromFile(); onTestFinished(() => process.kill(pid, ...)); expect(...);`
   - allow `const child = spawn(...); onTestFinished(() => child.kill(...)); expect(...);` when the spawn itself is the daemon start and cleanup is registered immediately;
   - reject `let pid; onTestFinished(() => kill(pid)); expect(...); pid = readPidFromFile();` and equivalent await/fetch variants.
4. Tighten helper analysis so arbitrary local wrappers are inspected or reported rather than automatically exempted. Keep an explicit allowlist for shared fixture internals that are supposed to start daemon processes.
5. Keep diagnostics actionable. Messages should explain whether the issue is:
   - direct daemon entrypoint outside approved helper;
   - detached daemon cleanup not bound before observation;
   - local wrapper hiding daemon startup; or
   - non-local/undocumented suppression.
6. Run:
   - `mise exec -- npm test -- --fresh tests/lint-daemon-test-guardrails.test.ts tests/lint-no-leaky-test-daemon.test.ts`
   - `mise exec -- kspec validate --refs --warnings-ok`
   - `mise exec -- kspec validate --completeness --warnings-ok`
7. If the full lint command is run, classify pre-existing unrelated lint debt separately from this task. Do not broaden this task into repository-wide lint cleanup.

#### In scope
- `no-leaky-test-daemon` rule logic and diagnostics.
- Tests needed to prove false negatives are fixed without new false positives.

#### Out of scope
- Fixing unrelated lint rules or warnings.
- Changing daemon runtime behavior.
- Changing test helpers except for allowed-helper naming exports if strictly necessary and covered by tests.

#### Validation
- Regression tests from `@task-add-guardrail-binding-wrapper-regressions` pass.
- Existing daemon guardrail tests pass.
- Unrelated subprocess allowed cases remain accepted.
- `mise exec -- npm test -- --fresh tests/lint-daemon-test-guardrails.test.ts tests/lint-no-leaky-test-daemon.test.ts`
- `mise exec -- kspec validate --refs --warnings-ok`
- `mise exec -- kspec validate --completeness --warnings-ok`

---
tasks.closed_reason: Merged to dev via detached reviewer merge helper after approved cycle 10 review. Summary: tightened no-leaky-test-daemon cleanup ownership and local helper-wrapper analysis, including object/class method wrapper coverage, with focused guardrail tests and full npm test passing.

notes.author: @claude
notes.content:
Approach: tightened the no-leaky-test-daemon rule on two fronts.

1) Cleanup-binding analysis: when a cleanup-registration callback (onTestFinished or process.on(<exit-event>)) is descended into for cleanup detection, also verify that every outer identifier the daemon-kill call captures (process.kill(pid, ...) / <handle>.kill('SIGTERM') / killPid(pid) / stopDaemon(pid)) is concretely bound at the registration site. A capture is bound when the binding is a parameter, a const/let/var declaration with a non-null/non-undefined initializer, or a top-level assignment with a non-null/non-undefined RHS that runs textually before the registration. Conditional/loop assignments do not count. Unbound captures cause the cleanup walker to reject the callback as cleanup, falling through to the missing-cleanup branch. A separate findUnboundCleanupClosure scanner runs in Program:exit so the diagnostic message can name the offending identifier (cleanupClosureUnbound).

2) Local wrapper boundary: removed the cleanup-timing exemption for detached starts nested inside local FunctionDeclarations / arrows / FunctionExpressions in non-allowlisted test files. The path allowlist (tests/helpers/daemon.ts, tests/helpers/mock-daemon.ts, tools/eslint-rules/, the two lint test files) is now the sole approved-fixture boundary; any detached start nested inside a local helper in an ordinary test file produces the localWrapperUnsafe diagnostic. The rule continues to early-return for path-allowlisted files, so the shared fixture remains exempt.

Test changes: flipped the eight it.fails(...) regressions in tests/lint-daemon-test-guardrails.test.ts back to it(...) per the documented contract — they pass now that the rule emits the expected diagnostics. The four allowed-narrow control tests stayed plain it(...) and still pass. Updated both describe-block docstrings to document the post-fix state.

Validation: full suite (8978 passed, 5 pre-existing skips); the focused lint suites pass with --fresh. No new no-leaky-test-daemon violations surface in tests/.

notes.author: Jacob Chapel
notes.content: [FIX_CYCLE: 1] Review verdict: changes_requested by reviewer-agent

notes.author: @claude
notes.content:
Fix cycle 2: addressed the cleanup-binding ownership blocker. The previous concretely-bound check accepted any non-null initializer (the reviewer's probe `const pid = 12345; runKspec("serve start --detach"); onTestFinished(() => process.kill(pid, "SIGTERM"))` passed because `pid` had a value, even though that value pre-dated the daemon start).

Added an ownership leg in tools/eslint-rules/no-leaky-test-daemon.js: cleanupCallbackBindingStatus now takes the detached-start node and rejects captures whose most recent concrete value-producing binding's source range ends BEFORE the detached-start begins. Parameters, class declarations, function declarations, and undeclared/global identifiers are not owned (they cannot represent the just-started daemon). The two safe shapes still pass: declarator ending after the start, and declarator whose initializer IS the start (e.g. `const child = spawn(...)` where the declarator's range encompasses the spawn). Threaded detachedStartNode through subtreeContainsDaemonCleanupCall, statementContainsCleanup, hasCleanupAfter, isInTryWithFinallyCleanup, findUnboundCleanupClosure, and scanForUnboundCleanupCallback. Diagnostic stays cleanupClosureUnbound — its message already names the ownership failure.

Added three regression tests in tests/lint-daemon-test-guardrails.test.ts (literal-pid-before-start, unrelated-spawn-child-handle-before-start, imported-pid). Re-verified the four existing safe shapes: pid captured AFTER the start, child handle captured by the spawn statement, let assigned after start before registration, let still null at registration with later assignment.

Validation: focused lint suites 225→228 tests pass. Full npm test 8982 passed (5 pre-existing skips, 1996.7s). kspec validate --refs and --completeness both pass with --warnings-ok.

notes.author: Jacob Chapel
notes.content: [FIX_CYCLE: 2] Review verdict: changes_requested by reviewer-agent

notes.author: @claude
notes.content:
Fix cycle 3: addressed the cycle-2 blocker on member-expression kill targets. The previous ownership check in tools/eslint-rules/no-leaky-test-daemon.js only inspected bare-Identifier targets in collectDaemonKillCaptureNames, so the reviewer probe `const holder = {}; runKspec("serve start --detach"); onTestFinished(() => { if (holder.pid !== undefined) process.kill(holder.pid, "SIGTERM"); }); expect(true).toBe(true); holder.pid = 12345;` was silently accepted as scoped cleanup.

Added extractRootCaptureIdentifierName(node) which unwraps ChainExpression and walks MemberExpression chains down to a root Identifier; returns null when the chain bottoms out in something that is not an Identifier (Literal, CallExpression, ThisExpression, TemplateLiteral, etc.). Threaded the helper through collectDaemonKillCaptureNames so process.kill(<expr>, ...), <expr>.kill("SIGTERM"), and killPid/stopDaemon/stopMockDaemon(<expr>, ...) all extract the root identifier (or push the UNVERIFIABLE_KILL_TARGET sentinel when no root is reachable). The cleanup-binding loop in cleanupCallbackBindingStatus rejects the sentinel up front so non-Identifier-rooted kill targets cannot bypass the check.

Added five regression tests in tests/lint-daemon-test-guardrails.test.ts: process.kill(holder.pid) where holder predates the start, deep state.daemon.pid chain rooted in a pre-start binding, handle.child.kill("SIGTERM") member-receiver where handle predates the start, process.kill(getStalePid()) call-expression target rejected as unverifiable, and an allowed-narrow control where const child = spawn("kspec", ["serve", "start", "--detach"]) makes process.kill(child.pid, "SIGTERM") still accepted because the root child declarator range encompasses the spawn that IS the detached start.

Re-verified the four existing safe shapes (pid bound after the start, child handle captured by spawn, let-with-later-assign, and the path-allowlisted shared fixture) plus the prior cycle-7 ownership probes (literal-pid-before-start, unrelated-spawn-child-handle-before-start, imported-pid).

Validation: focused lint suites 228 -> 233 passing tests with --fresh. Full npm test 8987 passing (5 pre-existing skips). kspec validate --refs and --completeness both pass with --warnings-ok (warnings are pre-existing repository-wide debt unrelated to this task).

notes.author: Jacob Chapel
notes.content: [FIX_CYCLE: 3] Review verdict: changes_requested by reviewer-agent

notes.author: @claude
notes.content:
Fix cycle 4: addressed both cycle-3 blockers in tools/eslint-rules/no-leaky-test-daemon.js.

Blocker 1 (cleanupCallbackBindingStatus skipped callback-local targets): added callbackLocalKillTargetIsDynamic which walks the cleanup callback body, applies isStaticLiteralExpression to every VariableDeclarator init and AssignmentExpression RHS that targets the kill identifier, and rejects when every source is literal-only. Parameters are also rejected because the cleanup framework passes no useful arguments. The reviewer probe (callback-local const pid = 12345 + process.kill(pid, ...)) now emits cleanupClosureUnbound.

Blocker 2 (extractRootCaptureIdentifierName left TS wrappers unverifiable): extracted unwrapTransparentExpression as a fixed-point loop over ChainExpression, ParenthesizedExpression, TSAsExpression, TSSatisfiesExpression, TSNonNullExpression, TSTypeAssertion, and TSInstantiationExpression. The unwrap runs both before the MemberExpression descent and between unwraps, so stacked wrappers and wrapped member chains both resolve to the underlying root Identifier. The reviewer probe (process.kill(pid as number, SIGTERM) over a pid captured after the start) is now accepted.

Same isStaticLiteralExpression and unwrapTransparentExpression helpers are used by both fixes, so the AST treatment is consistent — wrapped literals on callback-local targets resolve as static, wrapped identifiers on captured kill targets resolve to the root.

Added eight regression tests in tests/lint-daemon-test-guardrails.test.ts: literal const init (rejected), let + literal assign (rejected), TS-asserted literal (rejected), CallExpression init (allowed), TS as-cast (allowed), TS non-null assertion (allowed), stacked TS wrappers (allowed), TS-cast over a pre-start member-expression root (rejected via recovered root). All cycle-7/8/9 ownership probes still pass.

Validation: focused lint suites 233 -> 241 passing tests with --fresh; full npm test 2418 suites passed (8995 passed, 5 pre-existing skips, 2009.5s); kspec validate --refs and --completeness pass with --warnings-ok (warnings unchanged from pre-existing repository debt).

notes.author: Jacob Chapel
notes.content: [FIX_CYCLE: 4] Review verdict: changes_requested by reviewer-agent

notes.author: @claude
notes.content:
Fix cycle 5: addressed the cycle-4 polarity blocker on callback-local kill targets in tools/eslint-rules/no-leaky-test-daemon.js. Root cause was the cycle-4 callbackLocalKillTargetIsDynamic helper accepting non-literal RHS as 'plausibly dynamic' ownership; per ac-detached-cleanup-bound-before-observation that defers ownership to teardown and an intervening assertion failure leaves the cleanup with no captured target. The reviewer's manual probe (runKspec('serve start --detach') + onTestFinished(() => { const pid = readPidFromFile(); process.kill(pid, 'SIGTERM'); }) + expect) was accepted as cleanup; that was the bug.

Implementation: removed the dynamic-RHS exemption from cleanupCallbackBindingStatus — when isLocalToCallback(name, callbackFn) returns true, always emit cleanupClosureUnbound naming the offender. Removed the now-dead callbackLocalKillTargetIsDynamic and isStaticLiteralExpression helpers (197 lines). Diagnostic message already names the registration-time ownership requirement and points at the right fix (capture into outer const before the registration call).

Test updates: tests/lint-daemon-test-guardrails.test.ts:4275 flipped from expects-allowed to expects-flagged with cycle-4 reviewer-probe wording. Added three regression tests — callback-local MemberExpression init (state.lastPid as number, deferred read), callback-local let + dynamic CallExpression assign, and the safe alternative (read pid OUTSIDE callback after start, register closure that captures the outer const so ownership holds at registration time).

Production test: tests/cli-serve.test.ts 'does NOT silently fall back to [::1]' restructured to read the stale pid before registering cleanup. The daemon parent in --detach mode polls up to 5s for the child's pid file before exiting, and the daemon child writes the pid file before app.listen() is attempted, so by the time runKspec returns the pid file's existence is determined and the read-outside-callback pattern catches the same pids the prior read-inside pattern did.

Validation: focused lint suites 241 -> 244 passing tests with --fresh (3 net new regression tests); full npm test 2418 suites / 8995 -> 8998 passing tests (5 pre-existing skips, 2042.6s); kspec validate --refs and --completeness both pass with --warnings-ok. Manual oxlint AC probe against the cycle-4 reviewer source: runKspec('serve start --detach') + onTestFinished callback-local readPidFromFile() + later expect now exits 1 with cleanupClosureUnbound on 'pid' (was 0/no warnings). Safe alternative (read pid outside, capture in closure) accepted (exit 0).

notes.author: Jacob Chapel
notes.content: [FIX_CYCLE: 5] Review verdict: changes_requested by reviewer-agent

notes.author: @claude
notes.content:
Fix cycle 6: addressed the cycle-5 blocker on TS-wrapped null/undefined initializers in tools/eslint-rules/no-leaky-test-daemon.js. Root cause: isNullOrUndefinedInitializer only matched bare Literal null, Identifier undefined, and UnaryExpression void; TSAsExpression / TSSatisfiesExpression / TSNonNullExpression / TSTypeAssertion / TSInstantiationExpression / ParenthesizedExpression / ChainExpression around those nodes (e.g. const pid = undefined as number | undefined) escaped the placeholder check, so the declarator was treated as concretely value-producing and the cleanup closure was accepted even though the runtime value at registration time was still undefined.

Fix: call unwrapTransparentExpression at the top of isNullOrUndefinedInitializer (same fixed-point loop the kill-target analysis uses) before the structural classification. The unwrap is shared between the declarator-init leg and the assignment-RHS leg of findConcreteBindingInStatements / inspectStatementsForBinding, so wrapped placeholders are caught regardless of whether the binding is initialised at declaration or reassigned later. The hoisted nested-function-declaration order keeps the call site valid even though unwrapTransparentExpression is defined later in the file.

Test changes: added five regression tests in tests/lint-daemon-test-guardrails.test.ts under the cleanup-bound-before-observation describe — const pid = undefined as number | undefined (rejected), const pid = null as any (rejected), const pid = (undefined)! as number (rejected, stacked wrappers), let pid with post-start pid = undefined as any assignment (rejected), and a positive control const pid = readPidFromFile() as number after the start (accepted — wrapped concrete read stays concrete).

Validation: focused lint suites 244 -> 249 passing tests with --fresh; full npm test 2418 suites / 9003 passing tests (5 pre-existing skips, 2131.4s); kspec validate --refs and --completeness both pass with --warnings-ok (warnings unchanged from pre-existing repository debt). Manual oxlint AC probe against the cycle-5 reviewer source: const pid = undefined as number | undefined exits 1 with cleanupClosureUnbound on pid; const pid = null as any same; safe const pid = readPidFromFile() as number exits 0.

notes.author: Jacob Chapel
notes.content: [FIX_CYCLE: 6] Review verdict: changes_requested by reviewer-agent

notes.author: @claude
notes.content:
Fix cycle 7: addressed the cycle-6 blocker on direct try/finally finalizer cleanup bypassing ownership analysis in tools/eslint-rules/no-leaky-test-daemon.js. Root cause: subtreeContainsDaemonCleanupCall only invoked cleanupCallbackBindingStatus when descent crossed a registered-callback boundary, so a direct daemon-kill in a finalizer reached `if (isDaemonCleanupCallExpression(node)) return true;` on shape alone. The reviewer's manual probe (let pid; try { runKspec("serve start --detach"); expect(true).toBe(true); pid = readPidFromFile(); } finally { process.kill(pid as number, "SIGTERM"); }) was accepted as cleanup; that was the bug.

Implementation: added findDirectCleanupRegistrationUseNode and directCleanupCallOwnsDetachedDaemon helpers. The direct-cleanup branch of subtreeContainsDaemonCleanupCall now runs the same ownership rules as the registered-callback path (concrete binding at registration site AND binding range[1] >= detachedStart), with the implicit registration site set to the enclosing TryStatement (control crosses that boundary before any in-try throw can fire the finalizer). When no enclosing try is found, the call itself is the registration. UNVERIFIABLE_KILL_TARGET still rejects non-Identifier-rooted targets up front.

Diagnostic: added findUnboundDirectCleanupCapture / scanFinalizerForUnboundDirectCleanup as a parallel to findUnboundCleanupClosure so Program:exit emits cleanupClosureUnbound naming the offending capture for the finalizer case too. The diagnostic message text already covers both registration shapes since the underlying ownership rule is the same.

Test changes: added six regression tests in tests/lint-daemon-test-guardrails.test.ts under the cleanup-bound-before-observation describe — cycle-6 probe (rejected), undeclared free pid (rejected), stale pre-start literal pid (rejected), MemberExpression root predating start (rejected), pid bound after start before try (allowed-narrow), const child = spawn before try (allowed-narrow). The pre-existing tests/lint-no-leaky-test-daemon.test.ts "should allow serve start --detach in try/finally with cleanup" used an undeclared free `pid`; the cycle-6 ownership leg correctly rejects that, so updated the test to capture pid into a const between the start and the try block (the canonical safe shape).

Validation: focused lint suites 249 -> 255 passing tests with --fresh; full npm test 2419 suites / 9011 passing tests (5 pre-existing skips, 2001.2s); kspec validate --refs and --completeness both pass with --warnings-ok (warnings unchanged from pre-existing repository debt). Manual oxlint AC probe against the cycle-6 reviewer source: exit 1 with cleanupClosureUnbound on `pid` (was 0/no warnings). Safe alternative (pid bound before try) exits 0.

notes.author: Jacob Chapel
notes.content: [FIX_CYCLE: 7] Review verdict: changes_requested by reviewer-agent

notes.author: @claude
notes.content:
Fix cycle 8: addressed the cycle-7 blocker on direct try/finally finalizer cleanup using the enclosing TryStatement as the binding deadline in tools/eslint-rules/no-leaky-test-daemon.js. Root cause: findDirectCleanupRegistrationUseNode returned the TryStatement, so the ownership check required the binding to predate the try keyword and rejected the canonical safe shape where pid is captured inside the try body before the first observation.

Fix in three parts:

1. findDirectCleanupRegistrationUseNode now takes the detached start node. When the start is inside the try body, it locates the FIRST observation (await/expect/daemon URL fetch/WebSocket) in the try body after the start and uses that as the implicit registration deadline. If no in-try observation exists, the cleanup call itself is the deadline. This matches the registered-callback shape where ownership is checked at the onTestFinished registration call.

2. The binding analysis (walkStatementsForBinding and walkStatementsForConcreteBinding) descends into TryStatement.block and TryStatement.finalizer on the unconditional execution path so cross-scope shapes (let pid; declared outer, pid = ... assigned inside the try) resolve to the in-try assignment as the concrete binding. Previously the outer-scope walker only saw the let-with-no-init.

3. subtreeContainsDaemonCleanupCall now carries an inFinalizerContext flag (set by isInTryWithFinallyCleanup and the TryStatement.finalizer recursion path). When set, the walker descends through defensive-guard conditionals so "if (pid !== undefined) process.kill(pid, SIGTERM)" inside a finalizer is recognised. Ownership analysis on each daemon-cleanup CallExpression still gates whether the call counts as cleanup, so the guard is hygiene rather than load-bearing safety.

Test changes: five regression tests added in tests/lint-daemon-test-guardrails.test.ts under the cleanup-bound-before-observation describe -- cycle-8 safe-ordering with if guard (allowed-narrow), cycle-8 safe-ordering no guard (allowed-narrow), no in-try observation (allowed-narrow), await-shaped unsafe variant (rejected), conditional-assignment unsafe variant (rejected). All cycle-7 reviewer's existing safe and unsafe probes still flag/accept correctly.

Validation: focused lint suites 255 -> 260 passing tests with --fresh; full npm test 2419 suites / 9016 passing tests (5 pre-existing skips, 2003.3s); kspec validate --refs and --completeness both pass with --warnings-ok (warnings unchanged from pre-existing repository debt). Manual oxlint probe against the cycle-7 reviewer source: unsafe finalizer (assignment AFTER expect) exits 1 with cleanupClosureUnbound on pid; safe finalizer with if guard (assignment BEFORE expect) exits 0; safe finalizer without guard exits 0.

notes.author: Jacob Chapel
notes.content: [FIX_CYCLE: 8] Review verdict: changes_requested by reviewer-agent

notes.author: @claude
notes.content:
Fix cycle 9: addressed the cycle-8 blocker on multi-start ownership in tools/eslint-rules/no-leaky-test-daemon.js. Root cause: isCaptureOwnedByDetachedStart only checked that the binding's range[1] >= detachedStartNode.range[0], so a single binding satisfied ownership for EVERY detached start whose position predated it — the reviewer's probe (runKspec("serve start --detach --port 3456"); runKspec("serve start --detach --port 3457"); const pid = readPidFromFile(); onTestFinished(() => process.kill(pid, "SIGTERM")); expect(true).toBe(true);) was accepted as scoped cleanup for both starts even though a single pid can only own one daemon.

Fix: added an intervening-start check inside isCaptureOwnedByDetachedStart. The predicate now iterates pendingDetachChecks and rejects the binding if any other detached start node has its source position strictly greater than detachedStart and less than or equal to bindingEnd. The window is exclusive on detachedStart (so the start being checked doesn't disqualify itself) and inclusive on bindingEnd (so an intervening start that ends right before the binding still counts). pendingDetachChecks is fully populated at Program:exit, which is when the cleanup analysis runs, so the lookup is sound.

Coverage: the same predicate flows through cleanupCallbackBindingStatus (registered onTestFinished path) and directCleanupCallOwnsDetachedDaemon (try/finally finalizer path), and the diagnostic scanners (findUnboundCleanupClosure, findUnboundDirectCleanupCapture) reuse it to surface the offending capture name. The diagnostic message is unchanged because the underlying ownership rule is the same — it just rejects more shapes now.

Added four regression tests in tests/lint-daemon-test-guardrails.test.ts under the cleanup-bound-before-observation describe — cycle-8 reviewer probe (rejected, anchored to port 3456), try/finally finalizer multi-start variant (rejected, anchored to port 3456), interleaved per-daemon onTestFinished cleanup with separate pidN bindings (allowed-narrow), and two const child = spawn(...) per-daemon bindings (allowed-narrow). The allowed-narrow tests guard against over-tightening: each declarator's range encompasses its own spawn or sits between the per-daemon start and registration, so the intervening-start check correctly accepts both bindings.

Validation: focused lint suites 260 -> 264 passing tests with --fresh; full npm test 2419 suites / 9020 passing tests (5 pre-existing skips, 2001.4s); kspec validate --refs and --completeness both pass with --warnings-ok (warnings unchanged from pre-existing repository debt). Manual oxlint probe against the cycle-8 reviewer source: exits 1 with cleanupClosureUnbound on pid, anchored to the FIRST runKspec call (port 3456). Single-start safe shape and per-daemon scoped cleanup shapes still exit 0.

notes.author: Jacob Chapel
notes.content: [FIX_CYCLE: 9] Review verdict: changes_requested by reviewer-agent

notes.author: @claude
notes.content:
Fix cycle 10: addressed the cycle-9 blocker on object-method and class-method helper boundary coverage in tools/eslint-rules/no-leaky-test-daemon.js. Root cause: isInHelperFunction only matched named FunctionDeclaration and VariableDeclarator+(FunctionExpression|ArrowFunctionExpression) bindings, so the cycle-9 reviewer probe (const daemonHelper = { start() { runKspec("serve start --detach --port 3456"); const pid = readPidFromFile(); onTestFinished(() => process.kill(pid, "SIGTERM")); } }; daemonHelper.start(); expect(true).toBe(true);) exited oxlint with no diagnostic. The wrapper hid the daemon startup behind an object shorthand method while satisfying the cleanup contract internally — but the call site never registered cleanup tied to the daemon, which violates ac-approved-daemon-helper-boundary-explicit.

Fix: when the walk encounters a FunctionExpression or ArrowFunctionExpression, the predicate now inspects its immediate parent and returns true for: Property whose value === function (object-property method bindings — shorthand and longhand), MethodDefinition whose value === function (class instance/static methods), PropertyDefinition whose value === function (class-field arrows/functions), and plain '=' AssignmentExpression whose right === function and left is Identifier or MemberExpression (assignment-to-binding helpers like helper.start = function () {}). The path allowlist still gates rule entry, so the shared fixture (tests/helpers/daemon.ts, mock-daemon.ts, the rule itself, and the lint test files) stays exempt. The localWrapperUnsafe diagnostic message was updated from 'function/arrow' to 'function, arrow, or method (object property, class method, or function reassigned to a binding)' so the message matches the AST shapes the predicate now covers.

Added eight regression tests in tests/lint-daemon-test-guardrails.test.ts under the existing 'local wrappers around detached daemon starts are not approved helpers' describe block: cycle-9 object-shorthand probe (rejected), longhand FunctionExpression property (rejected), arrow property (rejected), class instance method (rejected), static class method (rejected), class-field arrow (rejected), assignment-to-member (rejected), and an allowed-narrow control verifying that an object-shorthand method inside the path-allowlisted tests/helpers/daemon.ts is still exempt.

Validation: focused lint suites 264 -> 272 passing tests with --fresh; full npm test 2419 suites / 9028 passing tests (5 pre-existing skips, 2008.1s); kspec validate --refs and --completeness both pass with --warnings-ok (warnings unchanged from pre-existing repository debt). Manual oxlint probes for object-method-shorthand, class-method, longhand-fn-property, arrow-property, class-field-arrow, and assignment-to-member shapes all exit 1 with localWrapperUnsafe; the canonical safe inline shape (no wrapper, pid captured, onTestFinished registered) and the shared-fixture method shapes still exit 0.

tasks.title: Validate daemon hardening corrective work end to end
tasks.description:
## Task 6 — Validate daemon hardening corrective work end to end

Proposed slug: `task-validate-daemon-hardening-corrections`
Type: `task`
Priority: `P3`
Plan ref: `@plan-daemon-test-fixture-hardening`
Spec ref: `@daemon-test-guardrail-precision`
Additional related spec: `@daemon-test-startup-failure-hygiene`
Tags: `daemon-tests`, `validation`, `follow-up`
Depends on: `@task-fix-register-cleanup-failure-leak`, `@task-fix-guardrail-binding-wrapper-analysis`
Automation: leave unassessed until Jacob approves.

### Description

#### What
Run an end-to-end validation pass for the corrective daemon hardening work, align only the relevant spec implementation statuses when the tightened behavior is actually covered, and record validation evidence in this task's notes.

This task verifies that:

- the real daemon fixture stops owned children on cleanup-registration failure;
- the static guardrail reports unbound cleanup callbacks and arbitrary local wrappers;
- existing safe daemon fixture and guardrail cases still pass;
- the tightened specs are no longer overclaiming `implemented` status once the fixes land;
- no new daemon process leaks are left behind by the focused suites.

#### Why
The corrective work changes spec text, real daemon fixture cleanup, and static lint guardrail analysis. A final validation task prevents the same failure mode that motivated this follow-up: several individually plausible changes can combine into a still-incomplete or overclaimed result. Validation should explicitly check the tightened behavior and the original daemon-test fixture standardization spirit: tests should be isolated, deterministic, endpoint-aware, and protected by enforceable guardrails rather than relying on broad manual discipline.

#### How
1. Inspect the final specs:
   - `mise exec -- kspec item get @daemon-test-startup-failure-hygiene`
   - `mise exec -- kspec item get @daemon-test-guardrail-precision`
2. Confirm implementation/status alignment:
   - specs with all tightened ACs covered must be aligned to `implemented`;
   - specs with any remaining uncovered tightened ACs must stay or be set to `in_progress` or lower, with the uncovered ACs named in the task note;
   - do not mark either spec `implemented` solely because focused suites passed; the note must tie passing evidence to the actual tightened AC ids from `kspec item get`.
3. Run focused suites:
   - `mise exec -- npm test -- --fresh tests/helpers/daemon.test.ts`
   - `mise exec -- npm test -- --fresh tests/e2e-fixture-daemon-cleanup.test.ts`
   - `mise exec -- npm test -- --fresh tests/lint-daemon-test-guardrails.test.ts tests/lint-no-leaky-test-daemon.test.ts`
4. Run kspec validation:
   - `mise exec -- kspec validate --refs --warnings-ok`
   - `mise exec -- kspec validate --alignment --warnings-ok`
   - `mise exec -- kspec validate --completeness --warnings-ok`
5. Run the full test suite if runtime budget allows:
   - `mise exec -- npm test -- --fresh`
   If the full suite is skipped due runtime budget, record that explicitly in the task notes and include focused suite evidence instead.
6. Check process hygiene around the focused daemon suites:
   - capture a pre-suite daemon-process baseline;
   - run the focused daemon suites;
   - capture a post-suite daemon-process snapshot;
   - compare for new `kspec`/daemon child processes tied to the test temp directories, isolated homes, pid files, or command lines used by these suites.
   If existing unrelated daemon processes are present, classify them as pre-existing. Do not kill ambient user processes. If a new test-started daemon remains, record validation failure and keep statuses honest rather than fixing it in this task.
7. Verify worktree/shadow state:
   - `git status --short --branch`
   - `git -C .kspec status --short --branch`

notes.author: @claude
notes.content: Investigation. Original full-suite hang (180s timeout) on tests/daemon-build.test.ts could not be reproduced locally on a clean run (took 794ms in full suite). Root cause analysis: (1) Test calls plain fetch() against the just-spawned daemon with no AbortSignal; if a daemon is alive but stops responding mid-request, fetch hangs forever and only the outer 180s vitest timeout breaks it. (2) runCommand uses spawnSync with timeout 120s, but on timeout/non-zero exit the assertion only checks status — stdout/stderr are silently discarded, so the hang yields no diagnostics. (3) Whole describe wraps both runtimes in one big block with no per-step bound. Plan: bound each fetch with AbortSignal.timeout, surface build stdout/stderr on any non-success, and add per-step diagnostics so a hang fails fast with actionable output (which runtime, which fetch, what the daemon stderr says). Tightens determinism without weakening fixture coverage — same ACs still verified, just bounded.

notes.author: @claude
notes.content: Implementation. tests/daemon-build.test.ts now bounds every HTTP probe with AbortSignal.timeout(5s) and dumps daemon stdout/stderr tails plus per-step labels (runtime, step, url) on any failure. The build subprocess fails fast with stdout/stderr-tail dumps on non-zero exit, signal-kill, or spawn error — previously expect(result.status).toBe(0) discarded all output so a wedged build produced no diagnostics. Unbounded fetches were the strongest hang candidate: with no AbortSignal, a daemon that bound but stopped responding mid-request would only break on the outer 180s vitest timeout. Verified: focused run passes 2/2 in 862ms; full suite passes 8979 tests, daemon-build.test.ts ran in 791ms in heavy-serial pool. AC coverage unchanged — same fixture contract, runtime adapter, endpoint consistency, runtime selection, and mode boundary ACs remain annotated. No spec change needed: this is implementation hardening of an existing test, not new behavior.

tasks.title: Stabilize Bun websocket runtime parity startup hook
tasks.description: During review of @task-fix-register-cleanup-failure-leak on 2026-05-11, full npm test failed once in tests/daemon-api/websocket-protocol.test.ts:482: the Bun runtime parity case timed out in beforeEach after 60000ms. Immediate fresh reruns of tests/daemon-api/websocket-protocol.test.ts passed, so this appears flaky rather than introduced by the cleanup-registration fix. Investigate why Bun daemon startup or runtime availability/setup can occasionally exceed the hook budget under full-suite load, then make the test deterministic without masking real startup failures.

Reviewed one-file test-only change in tests/daemon-api/websocket-protocol.test.ts: parity beforeEach hook budget is now 90s and startTestDaemon readiness budget is explicitly 25s per probe, preserving bounded readiness while allowing DaemonReadinessError diagnostics to surface. Focused websocket protocol suite passed fresh, and the same suite passed inside the full npm test run. Full run exposed unrelated deterministic cli-no-daemon failure tracked separately as @01KS090W.

notes.author: @claude
notes.content:
Investigation:

Reproduced startup timing for both Node and Bun spawning dist/daemon/index.js with the fixture flow (isolated HOME, .kspec/ + shadow-detection pointer, e2e fixtures copied). In isolation on this host:
- Bun: health ~220ms, cache-ready ~280ms across 5 cold spawns
- Node: health ~270ms, cache-ready ~315ms across 3 cold spawns
- Even under simulated load (12 background workers churning node spawnSync), Bun stayed at ~220ms/280ms

So the daemon itself is not slow. The flake is structural to how the suite drives the daemon:

tests/daemon-api/websocket-protocol.test.ts has two describes:
  1. parent describe (lines 122-454) — 14 Node tests, each beforeEach spawns + tears down a real daemon
  2. runtime-parity describe (line 467+) — 2 tests × 2 runtimes (Node + Bun) in that order

By the time the parity describe's Bun beforeEach runs, the same test process has already cold-spawned/torn-down ~15-16 daemons. Process-table churn, port reuse, and IO contention pile up. The Bun parity beforeEach inherits these effects on top of:
  - createTestDaemonProject(): git init + fsCp recursive of e2e fixtures
  - spawn('bun', [dist/daemon/index.js, ...]) cold-start
  - startTestDaemon readiness: probeHealth 15s budget + probeCacheReady 15s budget (30s combined under default DEFAULT_TIMEOUT_MS)

The current beforeEach has hookTimeout=60_000 — only 30s of headroom above the readiness budget. Under accumulated full-suite IO contention this can be eaten by createTestDaemonProject + spawn cold-start, leaving the hook to fire before the readiness probe times out. The failure surfaces as a bare "beforeEach hook timed out after 60000ms" rather than a DaemonReadinessError with the diagnostic bundle (stdout/stderr/health/cache-status) — masking the actual failure stage and violating the spirit of @daemon-backed-test-fixture-contract ac-readiness-diagnostics.

Fix approach (test-only, no daemon code change):

1. Raise the parity beforeEach hook timeout from 60_000 → 90_000ms to match the parent describe's { timeout: 90_000 } intent. This guarantees the readiness probe always has room to surface DaemonReadinessError with diagnostics before the hook gets preempted.
2. Pass an explicit timeoutMs: 25_000 to startTestDaemon for parity tests (50s combined readiness budget). A real startup failure still throws DaemonReadinessError within 50s with full diagnostics; legitimate cold-start under contention (which empirically stays well under 30s) has ample headroom.
3. Update the inline comment to document why the budget is wider in the parity case (cumulative file-level daemon churn).
4. Apply the same change to both Node and Bun runtimes within the parity describe — the same structural issue affects whichever runtime runs later in the matrix; Bun happens to be it today but Node could be next if matrix order changes.

Why this does NOT mask failures:
- Readiness is still bounded (25s per probe, 50s combined). A daemon that genuinely fails to bind or load returns a DaemonReadinessError with the full diagnostic bundle (endpoint, runtime, pid, exit code, stdout/stderr tail, last health + cache-status responses) per the existing fixture contract.
- A spawn launch error (ENOENT / EACCES) still races readiness and surfaces immediately via the launch-error race in startTestDaemon.
- The hook timeout only fires if readiness diagnostics themselves take >40s to assemble, which would indicate a deeper process-level hang — that's exactly the kind of failure we want to surface as "the test infrastructure itself broke" rather than confuse it with a daemon-startup issue.

Test plan:
- npm test (full suite, fresh cache) — must pass cleanly; rerun multiple times to confirm Bun parity is no longer flaky
- Confirm the Bun parity test still asserts the same behavior (health.runtime, connect/subscribe/broadcast, heartbeat degradation log)

notes.author: @claude
notes.content:
Implementation complete (commit 2c98d77b4):

- Added explicit timeoutMs: 25_000 to startTestDaemon (50s combined health+cache readiness budget vs. prior 30s default)

tasks.title: Tighten daemon guardrail cleanup semantics specs
tasks.description:
What:
- Update the existing `@daemon-test-guardrail-precision` requirement with
  exact cleanup-effect and cleanup-boundary ACs so the guardrail contract
  cannot be satisfied by cleanup-shaped code that leaves a daemon alive.
- Add `ac-cleanup-operation-terminates-daemon` with this behavioral shape:
  Given a test starts a detached daemon through a daemon lifecycle path;
  When the guardrail evaluates cleanup for that daemon; Then only cleanup
  operations that terminate or stop the daemon satisfy the cleanup
  requirement.
- Add `ac-cleanup-probes-do-not-count` with this behavioral shape: Given a
  test starts a detached daemon and registers cleanup-shaped code; When the
  code only probes liveness, emits documentation text, calls a non-daemon
  helper, or sends a non-terminating signal; Then the detached daemon start
  is reported as missing scoped cleanup.
- Add `ac-cleanup-helper-origin-is-trusted` with this behavioral shape:
  Given a test cleanup callback calls a helper by a daemon-cleanup-like
  name; When that helper is locally defined or otherwise not one of the
  approved cleanup primitives; Then the helper name alone does not satisfy
  daemon cleanup.
- Add `ac-cleanup-registration-is-test-scoped` with this behavioral shape:
  Given a test starts a detached daemon; When cleanup is registered only on
  process-lifecycle or global shutdown hooks; Then that registration does
  not satisfy the per-test scoped cleanup requirement.
- Add `ac-implicit-autostart-cleanup-before-observation` with this
  behavioral shape: Given a test invokes a CLI command that may implicitly
  auto-start a daemon and then observes the started daemon's pid, metadata,
  process, or endpoint; When the test performs later assertions or daemon
  observations before registering cleanup for that daemon; Then the unsafe
  auto-started daemon ownership is reported.
- Set `@daemon-test-guardrail-precision` implementation status back to
  `in_progress` without cascading to unrelated specs.

Why:
The current guardrail precision spec covers ordering and binding, but it
does not say that credited cleanup must actually terminate the daemon, must
be trusted structurally, or must run at the current-test boundary. That
under-specification allowed `process.kill(pid, 0)`, local no-op `killPid`,
and `process.on("exit", ...)`-only cleanup to look compliant.

How:
- Use `kspec item ac add @daemon-test-guardrail-precision ...` for each new
  AC.
- Use exact behavioral wording above; do not encode file names or internal
  AST predicate names in the spec ACs.
- Run `mise exec -- kspec item get @daemon-test-guardrail-precision` and
  verify all new AC IDs are present once.
- Run `mise exec -- kspec validate --refs --warnings-ok`.

Testing:
- `mise exec -- kspec item get @daemon-test-guardrail-precision`
- `mise exec -- kspec validate --refs --warnings-ok`

Covers: @daemon-test-guardrail-precision ac-cleanup-operation-terminates-daemon,
ac-cleanup-probes-do-not-count, ac-cleanup-helper-origin-is-trusted,
ac-cleanup-registration-is-test-scoped,
ac-implicit-autostart-cleanup-before-observation

tasks.title: Add adversarial guardrail regressions for cleanup effects
tasks.description:
What:
- Extend `tests/lint-no-leaky-test-daemon.test.ts` and, where the newer
  harness is the better home, `tests/lint-daemon-test-guardrails.test.ts`
  with failing-before-fix regression cases for cleanup effect semantics.
- Add rejected cases for `onTestFinished(() => process.kill(pid, 0))`,
  `process.kill(pid, "SIGUSR1")`, `process.kill(pid, "SIGCONT")`, and any
  other non-terminating or daemon-irrelevant signal literals the rule can
  statically identify.
- Add rejected cases where a local no-op or unrelated helper named
  `killPid`, `stopDaemon`, or `stopMockDaemon` is called in a cleanup
  callback but does not invoke an approved terminating cleanup primitive.
- Add accepted cases for `process.kill(pid)`, `process.kill(pid,
  "SIGTERM")`, `process.kill(pid, "SIGKILL")`, and project-approved stop
  helpers whose origin or body proves they stop the just-started daemon.
- Add accepted and rejected cases for child-handle cleanup so
  `child.kill()` and `child.kill("SIGTERM")` are treated consistently with
  Node's terminating defaults while `child.kill("SIGUSR1")` remains
  rejected.
- Keep each synthetic snippet self-contained and assert on the rule message
  instead of merely checking a non-zero parser exit.

Why:
The current rule accepts `process.kill(...)` by member-expression shape,
regardless of signal. A liveness probe such as `process.kill(pid, 0)` proves
the process exists but does not terminate it. Name-only helper recognition
has the same failure shape: a local function named `killPid` can be a no-op.

How:
- Place tests near the existing cleanup-timing and cleanup-callback
  adversarial cases so future reviewers can compare accepted and rejected
  shapes.
- Annotate each regression with the new `@daemon-test-guardrail-precision`
  AC it protects.
- For helper-origin cases, include at least one locally defined no-op helper
  and one approved helper/import case so the implementation cannot solve
  the false negative by banning all helpers.

Testing:
- First run the new cases and observe they fail against the current rule.

tasks.title: Fix guardrail cleanup-effect classification
tasks.description:
What:
- Update `tools/eslint-rules/no-leaky-test-daemon.js` so cleanup credit is
  based on terminating daemon cleanup, not merely cleanup-shaped syntax.
- For `process.kill(pid, signal)`, accept only missing/undefined signal or
  explicit terminating signals such as `SIGTERM`, `SIGKILL`, and `SIGINT`.
  Reject signal `0`, non-terminating signal literals, and unknown literal
  signals unless the rule has an explicit project reason to treat them as
  terminating.
- For child-handle `.kill(...)`, align the accepted signal policy with
  `process.kill`: no signal and known terminating signals count;
  non-terminating or daemon-irrelevant signals do not count.
- Stop treating bare helper names such as `killPid`, `stopDaemon`, or
  `stopMockDaemon` as sufficient when the helper is locally defined as a
  no-op or otherwise cannot be trusted. Either restrict recognition to
  approved imports/known helper paths or inspect the local helper body for a
  terminating daemon cleanup primitive.
- Preserve accepted cleanup through `kspec serve stop` lifecycle commands
  and approved shared helper internals.

Why:
The guardrail is supposed to prove that tests do not leak daemon processes.
A liveness probe, diagnostic signal, or local no-op helper does not stop the
daemon and therefore cannot be an exception to the detached-start rule.

How:
- Refactor the cleanup classifier into separate predicates for terminating
  signals, trusted helper calls, child-handle cleanup, process PID cleanup,
  and CLI `serve stop` cleanup.
- Keep the allowed signal list centralized and documented in the rule
  comment.
- When local helper-body inspection is used, avoid counting recursive
  wrappers or helper names whose body does not contain an approved
  terminating cleanup call.
- Keep current false-positive protections for string literals and
  non-daemon subprocesses.

Testing:
- `mise exec -- npm test -- --fresh tests/lint-no-leaky-test-daemon.test.ts tests/lint-daemon-test-guardrails.test.ts`
- `mise exec -- npm run lint` or the repository lint command that invokes
  oxlint, if available and not blocked by unrelated pre-existing lint
  failures.

Covers: @daemon-test-guardrail-precision ac-cleanup-operation-terminates-daemon,
ac-cleanup-probes-do-not-count, ac-cleanup-helper-origin-is-trusted;
@daemon-test-harness-guardrails ac-detached-serve-without-cleanup-flagged,
ac-exceptions-are-localized

notes.author: @claude
notes.content:
Fix cycle 6: addressed cycle-5 reviewer blocker @01KRE6ARGB5SF4YPG2F2MGZ51N (binding-order false negative).

Blocker: findLocalHelperDefinition trusted local helper definitions even when the declarator's binding was only initialized AFTER an intervening observation. The reviewer's synthetic probe was: runKspec(serve start --detach); const pid = readPidFromFile(); onTestFinished(() => killPid(pid)); expect(true).toBe(true); const killPid = (p) => process.kill(p, "SIGTERM"); — pre-fix output was Found 0 warnings because the lookup walked every statement in the enclosing block without considering source order, found the declarator, the body inspection saw process.kill, and the use site was silently credited. If the expect fails (or any intervening statement throws), teardown invokes the cleanup arrow while killPid is in TDZ — ReferenceError, daemon leaks.

Fix: in findLocalHelperDefinition, when matchHelperDefinitionInStatement returns a VariableDeclarator-with-function-init match, call statementIsVariableHelperDefinition+isStatementBeforeUseSite to verify the declarator's statement index is strictly less than the use site's containing statement index in the same enclosing block. If not, return LOCAL_BINDING_OPAQUE so isTrustedHelperByOrigin rejects via the explicit opaque branch. FunctionDeclarations are exempt because ES2015+ block-scoped function declarations are hoisted with their value to the start of the enclosing scope.

New helpers: statementIsVariableHelperDefinition (unwraps ExportNamed/Default wrappers, returns true for VariableDeclaration with simple-Identifier id and FunctionExpression/ArrowFunctionExpression init matching name); isStatementBeforeUseSite (strict less-than to keep pathological IIFE-init shapes opaque). Strict less-than means a declarator's containing statement that IS the use-site statement (e.g. const k = (() => { onTestFinished(() => k(p)); })()) is also opaque — conservatively safe.

Regressions: 5 positive flag-it (const arrow after, const function expression after, let arrow after, describe-scope const after afterEach, program-level const after describe block) plus 2 negative companions (hoisted FunctionDeclaration after registration is still accepted; const arrow declared before registration is still accepted).

Blocker: findLocalHelperDefinition walked function parameters and BlockStatement/Program statement lists only, so a ForStatement init (for (const killPid = (_p) => {}; ...) {...}), a ForOfStatement/ForInStatement left binding (for (const killPid of [(_p) => {}]) {...}), or a CatchClause param (catch (killPid) {...}) was invisible to the helper-origin check. notes.author: @claude
notes.content:
Fix cycle 9: addressed cycle-8 reviewer blockers @01KREK5KR988F5WVRCTFYV38G2 and @01KREK5T2TKFKM6VK682R8FACH on @01KREJR1 review.

Blocker 1 (line 1119): isHelperNameImportedFromApprovedPath trusted the LOCAL alias name plus resolved path, but never inspected which export was actually imported. `import { startTestDaemon as killPid } from "./helpers/daemon"` was credited as cleanup even though startTestDaemon is the daemon STARTER. Fix: anchor approved-import trust on the IMPORTED export name. New constant APPROVED_CLEANUP_HELPER_EXPORT_NAMES (= killPid / stopDaemon / stopMockDaemon — same names as TRUSTED_HELPER_NAMES but matched against spec.imported.name, not spec.local.name). Only ImportSpecifier (named imports) carry an `imported` field; ImportDefaultSpecifier and ImportNamespaceSpecifier shapes cannot be tied to a specific approved cleanup export and are rejected outright. Non-Identifier `imported` shapes (the proposal `import { "kill-pid" as killPid }` form) are also rejected.

Blocker 2 (line 1085): helper-body inspection accepted any terminating primitive in the body without inspecting its TARGET. `function killPid(_pid) { process.kill(12345, "SIGTERM"); }` always killed a hardcoded literal pid unrelated to whatever the call site passed. Fix: new isVerifiableKillTarget helper requires the kill target (the pid arg for process.kill, the receiver for <expr>.kill) to be an Identifier, ThisExpression, or non-computed MemberExpression chain rooted at one. Literal and computed targets (CallExpression, BinaryExpression, TemplateLiteral, computed MemberExpression) are rejected because they cannot represent the just-started daemon. Blocker 1 (line 1857 of cycle-10 head, strict primitive classifier rejected approved shared helper internals): the helper-body inspection required the body to reach process.kill / <child>.kill directly, so tests/cli-serve.test.ts's killPid(pid) — which delegates to stopPidBounded from ./helpers/process-stop — failed and repository lint reported 18 no-leaky-test-daemon errors on that file. tasks.title: Add adversarial guardrail regressions for cleanup boundaries
tasks.description:
What:
- Add failing-before-fix guardrail tests proving cleanup must be registered
  at a current-test cleanup boundary or in the same synchronous
  `try/finally` control flow that owns the daemon.
- Add rejected cases where the only cleanup registration is
  `process.on("exit", ...)`, `process.on("beforeExit", ...)`,
  `process.on("SIGTERM", ...)`, `process.once(...)`, `afterAll(...)`, or
  another process/global lifecycle hook that can leave the daemon alive
  while later tests run.
- Keep already-rejected cases for `beforeEach`, `beforeAll`, misplaced
  `afterEach`, callbacks assigned but never invoked, `Promise.finally`, and
  `queueMicrotask` covered and aligned with the new AC wording.
- Add accepted cases for `onTestFinished(() => terminatingCleanup(...))` and
  direct `try/finally` finalizers that are already bound to the concrete
  daemon pid or stop handle before observations can fail.
- Add a mixed case where a process-lifecycle fallback exists in addition to
  `onTestFinished`; the per-test cleanup should be what satisfies the
  guardrail, not the fallback.

Why:
Process-exit cleanup can be a last-resort safety net, but it is not scoped
to the test that started the daemon. Treating it as sufficient lets the
daemon survive subsequent tests and violates the fixture cleanup contract.

How:
- Update the existing process-on-exit allowed regression in
  `tests/lint-no-leaky-test-daemon.test.ts` so it becomes a rejected case
  under `ac-cleanup-registration-is-test-scoped`.
- Keep the failure message actionable: direct the author to
  `onTestFinished` or `try/finally`, not merely to any cleanup callback.
- Include comments explaining that process-lifecycle cleanup is allowed only
  as a supplemental fallback, not as the cleanup credit for the guardrail.

Testing:
- First run the new cases and observe the current `process.on("exit", ...)`
  allowed case fail the new expectation.
- After the implementation task, run:
  `mise exec -- npm test -- --fresh tests/lint-no-leaky-test-daemon.test.ts tests/lint-daemon-test-guardrails.test.ts`.

Covers: @daemon-test-guardrail-precision ac-cleanup-registration-is-test-scoped,
ac-detached-cleanup-before-observation, ac-detached-cleanup-bound-before-observation;
@daemon-test-harness-guardrails ac-detached-serve-without-cleanup-flagged

tasks.title: Fix guardrail cleanup-boundary classification
tasks.description:
What:
- Update `tools/eslint-rules/no-leaky-test-daemon.js` so process-lifecycle
  and global lifecycle hooks do not satisfy scoped cleanup for a daemon
  started inside a test.
- Treat `onTestFinished` and same-flow `try/finally` finalizers as the
  primary accepted cleanup boundaries for detached daemon starts.
- If a test also registers `process.on(...)` as a last-resort fallback, keep
  it allowed only when a valid per-test cleanup boundary is already present.
- Update diagnostics and rule comments that currently describe
  `process.on("exit"|...)` as valid cleanup.

Why:
The guardrail should prevent a daemon from remaining alive into later tests.
Process shutdown hooks run too late to provide that guarantee.

How:
- Remove process-exit event names from the predicate that credits cleanup.
- If useful, add a separate predicate for supplemental process fallbacks so
  comments and diagnostics can distinguish fallback safety nets from
  guardrail-satisfying cleanup.
- Verify local-disable exception behavior remains localized and
  behavior-specific.

tasks.title: Add bounded process-stop contract tests
tasks.description:
What:
- Add focused tests that prove daemon test cleanup observes process
  termination before reporting success and reaches a bounded outcome for
  uncooperative children.
- Cover the shared real-daemon fixture stop path in `tests/helpers/daemon.ts`
  using a test seam or synthetic child that ignores the initial termination
  signal and requires escalation.
- Cover the mock child-process daemon stop path in
  `tests/helpers/mock-daemon.ts` with a child that ignores `SIGTERM`.
- Cover PID-based cleanup used by CLI lifecycle tests, including signal exit
  races where `signalCode` is set and `exitCode` remains `null`.
- Assert that cleanup does not resolve until the child exit/death has been
  observed, or until a bounded failure diagnostic is surfaced.

Why:
Current cleanup helpers can send `SIGKILL` and then resolve from a timeout
callback without observing the child exit. That leaves a narrow but real
false success path where cleanup reports completion while the process still
exists.

How:
- Prefer small synthetic child scripts in temp directories over real daemon
  processes for uncooperative-signal tests.
- Use bounded event waits and process probes; do not add fixed sleeps except
  as explicit grace-period configuration under test.
- Add AC annotations for `@daemon-test-teardown-boundedness` and existing
  fixture contract ACs.

Testing:

  current cleanup helper behavior.
- After the implementation task, run:
  `mise exec -- npm test -- --fresh tests/helpers/daemon.test.ts tests/helpers/mock-daemon.test.ts tests/cli-serve.test.ts`.

notes.author: @claude
notes.content:
Added 5 failing-before-fix contract tests for bounded process-stop:

1. tests/helpers/daemon.test.ts — startTestDaemon stop() observes termination:
   Spawns a synthetic uncooperative Node script (ignores SIGTERM/SIGINT/SIGHUP)
   via __testBinaryOverride and a custom readiness probe that waits for a
   stdout handshake. Asserts that after started.stop() returns, the child
   exit event has been observed (exitCode or signalCode is non-null) AND
   the OS pid is no longer alive. Fails today because killChildScoped
   resolves from its setTimeout callback synchronously after kill('SIGKILL'),
   before libuv has fired the exit event.

2. tests/helpers/mock-daemon.test.ts — bounded child stop contract:
   Drives startMockDaemon({asChildProcess: true}) with a new --ignore-sigterm
   seam in mock-daemon.cjs that swaps the SIGTERM/SIGINT/SIGHUP handlers for
   no-ops. Asserts that after mock.stop() returns, the recorded pid is no
   longer alive. Fails today for the same reason as #1 — the stop closure
   finalizes from the SIGKILL-fallback timer callback rather than waiting
   for the actual exit event.

3-5. tests/cli-serve.test.ts — PID-based cleanup contract:
   Adds three regressions against the local killPid + waitForChildExit
   helpers using synthetic uncooperative children with a stdout handshake:
   - waitForChildExit must observe child exit before returning (same
     timer-callback bug as the daemon stop path).
   - waitForChildExit must take the fast-path for an already-signal-exited
     child (signalCode set, exitCode null). Currently the fast-path checks
     only exitCode !== null, so signal-exit handles wait the full 5s
     timeout before resolving.
   - killPid must drive an uncooperative pid to a bounded terminal outcome.
     Today killPid is fire-and-forget sync void — no escalation, no
     observation — so a SIGTERM-ignoring child survives indefinitely.

Source changes are minimal: one docstring update in tests/helpers/daemon.ts
(__testBinaryOverride now documented as both launch-failure simulation and
synthetic-child substitution), and a new test-only --ignore-sigterm flag in
tests/helpers/mock-daemon.cjs.

Key implementation detail: the synthetic child must finish installing its
signal handlers BEFORE the test sends any signals. Without a stdout
handshake, a too-fast SIGTERM races the script's handler installation,
hits the default terminate action, and masks the bug under test. All
five tests use the handshake pattern.

Verified: all 5 new tests fail today against the existing buggy helpers.
No existing tests in daemon.test.ts / mock-daemon.test.ts / cli-serve.test.ts
were broken (70 prior tests still pass).

tasks.title: Implement bounded process-stop primitives
tasks.description:
What:
- Add or refactor to a shared test-side process stop primitive used by the
  real daemon fixture, mock daemon child helper, CLI detached PID cleanup,
  and foreground child wait helpers where applicable.
- The primitive must send a graceful termination request, wait for observed
  exit/death, escalate to a forceful termination request when needed, and
  then wait again for observed exit/death before reporting success.
- If the process cannot be observed terminated after escalation, return or
  throw a bounded diagnostic instead of reporting successful cleanup.
- Treat signal-based exits as real exits even when `exitCode` remains
  `null` and only `signalCode` is set.
- Keep cleanup idempotent, and avoid killing unrelated processes when the
  owned child/PID has already exited.

Why:
Multiple helpers currently duplicate partial stop logic. Shared semantics
reduce future drift and make cleanup success mean the same thing for real
daemon, mock daemon, and CLI lifecycle tests.

How:
- Inspect `tests/helpers/daemon.ts`, `tests/helpers/mock-daemon.ts`, and
  `tests/cli-serve.test.ts` for existing stop helpers before choosing the
  shared helper location.
- Preserve existing public helper return shapes unless tests prove a more
  explicit diagnostic type is needed.
- Update comments and diagnostics to say cleanup observes termination rather

notes.author: @claude
notes.content:
Approach: introduce shared test-side helper tests/helpers/process-stop.ts with two entry points:

1. stopChildProcessBounded(child, opts) — for ChildProcess handles owned by daemon.ts and mock-daemon.ts. Sends graceful signal (SIGTERM), waits for observed exit (exitCode OR signalCode non-null OR 'exit' event fired) within graceful budget, escalates to SIGKILL on timeout, then waits again for observed exit within escalation budget. Treats signalCode-only exits as real exits.

2. stopPidBounded(pid, opts) — for PID-only callers in cli-serve.test.ts. Same graceful->escalate semantics, observes termination via process.kill(pid, 0) polling since no ChildProcess handle exists.

Both return Promise<void> on success and throw a BoundedStopError with diagnostics if escalation timeout elapses without observed exit. Idempotent (already-exited fast-path); avoid killing unrelated PIDs by checking liveness before each signal.

Refactor sites:
- daemon.ts killChildScoped -> use stopChildProcessBounded
- mock-daemon.ts inline stop() closures (both startup-failure cleanup and operational stop) -> use stopChildProcessBounded
- cli-serve.test.ts killPid + waitForChildExit -> retain helpers as thin wrappers around the new primitives so onTestFinished call sites keep their fire-and-forget shape while gaining bounded semantics. waitForChildExit will route through the same observed-exit logic so signalCode fast-path is honored.

tasks.title: Stabilize flaky file-lock concurrent write test
tasks.description: During review of @01KRCRJPMHMHC410TKRC5Y9HF1, full npm test -- --fresh failed once in tests/file-lock.test.ts:202: expected count: 5 but got count: 4 in 'File Lock should handle concurrent writes to same file safely'. Immediate rerun of npm test -- --fresh tests/file-lock.test.ts passed (21/21), so this appears intermittent rather than caused by the lint-rule branch. tasks.closed_reason: Merged to dev via detached reviewer helper. Reviewed and approved atomic pid-file publication in src/parser/file-lock.ts; targeted file-lock tests and full fresh npm test passed.

notes.author: @claude
notes.content:
Root cause: fs.writeFile(pidFile, marker) is not JS-atomic — internally it calls open(O_TRUNC) → write → close, each as an awaited libuv operation. While the writeFile is pending, a concurrent same-process staleness check could read the pid file BETWEEN open (which truncates) and write, see empty content, parse pid as NaN, fall through to the 'corrupt pid file' branch in checkStaleLock that returns stale=true, then rm the lockDir and acquire its own lock. That let two callers enter the critical section together, losing an increment.

Reproduced the race with a standalone harness driving the same 5-worker contention as tests/file-lock.test.ts:179 — saw 1 failure in 200 runs at baseline.

Fix: publish pidFile atomically via temp + rename. fs.writeFile to pid.tmp.<uuid> in the lockDir, then fs.rename to pid. Rename is atomic on POSIX, so concurrent readers either see ENOENT (notStale via existing catch) or the complete marker. On writeFile/rename error, rm the lockDir so we don't leave a stuck lock with no pid file.

Verified: 500 passes/500 at 10 same-process workers via repro; vitest concurrent-writes test passed 100/100 consecutive runs; full file-lock suite passed 20/20; full npm test --fresh passed (9072 passed, 5 skipped). No spec changes — this fixes a bug that violated the existing serialization contract from @scoped-dispatch-shadow-serialization.

tasks.title: Add cleanup preservation and no-blind-deletion ACs
tasks.description:
Add cleanup-policy acceptance criteria for active, in-flight, and
provisioning artifact preservation, consistent protection across destructive
cleanup surfaces, and no-blind-deletion behavior when protection state cannot be
trusted.

Why: @dispatch-workspace-cleanup-policy ac-4 protects active invocation
ownership for branch deletion, but the incident involves multiple artifact
surfaces and the in-flight/provisioning window before active registration.
The cleanup contract must make preservation path-independent and conservative
when ownership/protection state is unavailable, while remaining compatible with existing policy that may deterministically block or clean untrusted metadata after classification.

What: Add these exact ACs to @dispatch-workspace-cleanup-policy.

AC id: ac-active-inflight-provisioning-artifact-preserved
Given: Artifact cleanup evaluates a dispatcher-managed worktree, reviewer
  snapshot, root directory, or dispatch branch for work that is active,
  in-flight, or in provisioning.
When: Cleanup determines whether that artifact is eligible for destructive
  removal.
Then: Cleanup preserves the artifact instead of removing, pruning, or
  deleting it.

AC id: ac-protection-applies-to-every-destructive-surface
Given: Artifact cleanup discovers the same protected task or workspace
  through any destructive cleanup surface.
When: Cleanup evaluates worker worktrees, reviewer snapshots, root
  directories, workspace records, or dispatch branches.
Then: The protected artifact receives the same preserve outcome regardless
  of which cleanup surface discovered it.

AC id: ac-ambiguous-protection-blocks-blind-deletion
Given: Artifact cleanup cannot load or trust the registry, metadata, or
  protection state needed to classify whether a dispatcher-managed artifact
  is protected or safely cleanup-eligible.
When: The artifact would otherwise be considered eligible for destructive
  cleanup.
Then: Cleanup does not blindly delete the artifact; it reconstructs or
  reattaches trusted state, blocks cleanup with actionable guidance, or
  proceeds only after existing cleanup policy classification determines the
  metadata is untrusted and cleanup is safe.

...` for each AC. Set @dispatch-workspace-cleanup-policy implementation
status to in_progress with `--no-cascade` unless current evidence proves all

tasks.title: Centralize dispatch artifact protection decisions
tasks.description:
Introduce a single protection-policy helper for dispatch artifact cleanup and
route destructive cleanup decisions through that helper.

Why: The race can reappear if branch cleanup, root-directory pruning,
reviewer snapshot cleanup, and workspace-record reaping each use separate
protection logic. A shared policy is the long-term maintenance guardrail: new
cleanup surfaces must consume the same active/in-flight/provisioning decision
instead of inventing their own eligibility checks.

What:
1. In `src/agent-runtime/workspace.ts`, add an internal helper such as
   `buildDispatchArtifactProtectionState(...)` or
   `shouldPreserveDispatchArtifact(...)` that accepts resolved dispatch
   config, registry records/metadata, and active/in-flight task refs.
2. The helper must treat these as protection sources:
   - task refs supplied by cleanup callers as active/in-flight protection;
   - non-closed registry records while they still represent protected or
     unclassified work, including lifecycle_state `provisioning`, `ready`,
     `active`, `stale`, `integrating`, and `cleanup_blocked`; `closing`
     records are protected only while active/in-flight/provisioning
     ownership or unresolved integration remains, and otherwise may proceed
     through scheduled `reapDispatchWorkspace()` cleanup once classification
     says cleanup is eligible; generic orphan-branch pruning still preserves
     non-closed registry branches;
   - metadata-backed worktrees that can be recovered or classified before
     deletion.
3. The helper must return enough information for cleanup to preserve worker
   worktrees, reviewer worktrees/snapshots, unregistered root-directory
   candidates equal to or contained by protected paths, and dispatch
   branches belonging to protected records or unclassified records that have
   not yet been determined cleanup-eligible.
4. Registry or metadata load/parsing failure must produce a no-blind-deletion
   result for dispatcher-managed artifacts unless existing cleanup policy
   classification can determine that cleanup is safe. The result must
   include actionable diagnostic text for logs/test assertions.
5. Replace ad hoc protection checks inside `reconcileDispatchWorkspaceArtifacts()`
   with calls to this helper or helper-derived protected sets.

How: Keep the helper local to workspace cleanup unless other code needs it.
Do not add durable lease schema or owner/TTL fields. Preserve existing cleanup
behavior for records that are explicitly closed or terminal cleanup-eligible
after classification.

Testing: Add focused helper-level tests in `tests/dispatch-workspace-cleanup.test.ts`
or a new `tests/dispatch-artifact-protection.test.ts` proving preserve/delete
decisions for active, in-flight, provisioning/protected-unclassified,
closing cleanup-eligible, closed, and registry-unavailable cases.

Covers: @dispatch-workspace-cleanup-policy ac-active-inflight-provisioning-artifact-preserved,
ac-protection-applies-to-every-destructive-surface,
ac-ambiguous-protection-blocks-blind-deletion; @dispatch-workspace-registry
ac-partial-provisioning-classified-before-cleanup.

tasks.title: Apply protection policy across artifact reconciliation surfaces
tasks.description:
Ensure every destructive path in `reconcileDispatchWorkspaceArtifacts()` and
the cleanup paths it calls honors active, in-flight, and provisioning
protection.

Why: The original failure can reappear through any cleanup surface that
bypasses protection: metadata-less worktree removal, reviewer snapshot
cleanup, root-directory pruning, cleanup-eligible record reaping, or orphan
dispatch branch deletion.

What:
1. In `src/agent-runtime/workspace.ts`, before removing metadata-less
   dispatch worktrees, consult the shared protection decision and preserve
   artifacts that can be associated with active/in-flight/provisioning work
   or that cannot be classified safely.
2. Before calling `reapDispatchWorkspace()`, skip or block records whose task
   ref is active/in-flight or whose registry state is provisioning, protected, or unclassified
   until classification says the record is cleanup-eligible. Do not treat
   `closing` alone as protected when existing cleanup prerequisites are met
   and no active/in-flight/provisioning ownership remains.
3. Before deleting reviewer snapshot worktrees, preserve paths associated
   with protected records or active/in-flight task refs.
4. Before deleting unregistered root directories without `.git`, preserve
   candidates equal to or contained by protected worker/reviewer paths, and
   avoid blind deletion for ambiguous dispatcher-managed candidates when
   protection state is unavailable unless classification determines cleanup
   is safe.
5. Before deleting dispatch branches, preserve branches tracked by protected
   or unclassified records and avoid blind deletion when the registry cannot
   be loaded or trusted unless existing cleanup classification has
   determined the branch is safely cleanup-eligible.
6. Ensure diagnostics identify the cleanup surface and protection source when
   an artifact is preserved or blocked.

How: Preserve existing behavior for truly orphaned artifacts, for scheduled
`reapDispatchWorkspace()` cleanup of `closing` records after classification,
and for closed records that are cleanup-eligible under existing retention
rules. Orphan dispatch-branch pruning must still honor the existing
registry contract that preserves branches for non-closed records; branch
deletion for a closing workspace belongs to scheduled/bounded reaping, not to
the generic orphan-branch sweep. Avoid a broad grace-period heuristic as the
primary fix; use explicit protection state instead.

Testing: Update `tests/dispatch-workspace-cleanup.test.ts` and/or
`tests/dispatch-workspace-registry.test.ts` to cover each destructive surface
with both protected and cleanup-eligible negative-control cases.

Covers: @dispatch-workspace-cleanup-policy ac-active-inflight-provisioning-artifact-preserved,
ac-protection-applies-to-every-destructive-surface,
ac-ambiguous-protection-blocks-blind-deletion; @dispatch-workspace-registry
ac-partial-provisioning-classified-before-cleanup.

tasks.description: Full-suite review run for @01KRF37XVT9YSRGV87660W7BR6 failed once in tests/helpers/daemon.test.ts: startTestDaemon readiness diagnostics reports a diagnostic bundle when readiness times out. notes.author: @claude
notes.content:
Root cause: sampleEndpointDiagnostic in tests/helpers/daemon.ts:543 takes a single snapshot at failure time. Under heavy parallel load, a daemon spawned with a custom always-false probe (failingTimeoutMs=800) may not have bound to its port within the readiness budget, so the post-timeout fetch returns ECONNREFUSED ('fetch failed'). The diagnostic bundle then reports {error:...} instead of the expected 200, even though the daemon process is alive.

Approach: Add bounded retries inside sampleEndpointDiagnostic. When the caller passes a child handle and the child is alive (pid set, exitCode/signalCode null), retry the sample on transient fetch failures up to a budget (5s, 100ms interval). When the child is observably dead or no handle is provided, return the latest error immediately. This preserves the bundle-reflects-failure-time semantics while eliminating the race between daemon bind and diagnostic sample.

Spec coverage: existing ac-readiness-diagnostics says 'failure output reports a diagnostic bundle' — the fix strengthens the implementation to reliably surface the daemon's actual reachability state, no AC change required.

notes.author: @claude
